course.title: Cybersecurity
course.description: A defensive course on how systems are attacked and protected, from risk and threat modelling to web security, identity, cryptography and incident response.
course.audience: A capable adult with basic computing and networking knowledge, who may have tried hands-on labs such as Kali exercises but not studied the foundations. Practice is described only in authorised labs.

paragraphs: Many successful attacks on computer systems rely on ordinary faults: a password that was reused on another site, a flaw whose published fix nobody applied, or a server that returned a record without asking who wanted it. Each of these could have been found by a defender first. Cybersecurity is the work of finding such faults before someone else does, deciding which of them matter most, and noticing quickly when one has been used.

Much of that work can be measured. The cost of a risk is the cost of one incident multiplied by how often it is expected, the strength of a password against guessing is the number of possible passwords set against the speed of the guesser, and the protection given by several controls in a row is the product of what each one lets through. A firewall rule set, a certificate chain or a few lines of log can be read just as exactly, so once you know what each part means you can judge a system's defences from the evidence in front of you.

Attacks are described here only as far as a defender needs to recognise and stop them, and no working exploit code is given. Trying any technique belongs only on systems where you have permission, such as machines you own and training labs built for practice.
outcomes: You'll be able to classify a failure by confidentiality, integrity or availability and justify a control with annualised loss.
You'll be able to threat model a small system with STRIDE.
You'll be able to read a firewall rule set, a port scan and a log for signs of attack.
You'll be able to recognise injection, broken access control, CSRF and SSRF and name the fix.
You'll be able to judge a password scheme, a token and a certificate chain.
You'll be able to run the first hour of an incident by the NIST lifecycle.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems and How Computers and Networks Work.

modules.title: Foundations and threats
modules.description: What security protects, how risk is reasoned about, how to model a system's threats, and how attacks proceed.

modules.title: Network and web security
modules.description: How networks are segmented and defended, and the classes of flaw that most often break web applications.

modules.title: Identity and cryptography
modules.description: Proving who someone is, deciding what they may do, and the cryptographic tools underneath.

modules.title: Vulnerabilities and response
modules.description: Finding and fixing weaknesses, seeing attacks in logs, and handling an incident by the book.

concepts.title: CIA triad
concepts.summary: Confidentiality (only authorised readers), integrity (no unauthorised change) and availability (usable when needed).

concepts.title: Risk
concepts.summary: The combination of how likely a harmful event is and how much it would cost.

concepts.title: Annualised loss expectancy
concepts.summary: Single loss expectancy multiplied by annual rate of occurrence.

concepts.title: Data-flow diagram
concepts.summary: A picture of processes, data stores, external entities and flows, with trust boundaries where privilege changes.

concepts.title: STRIDE
concepts.summary: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.

concepts.title: Mitigation
concepts.summary: A design or control chosen to reduce a threat: remove it, reduce it, transfer it or accept it.

concepts.title: Attack stages
concepts.summary: Reconnaissance, initial access, execution, persistence, privilege escalation, lateral movement and impact; each gives a chance to detect.

concepts.title: Defence in depth
concepts.summary: Several independent controls, so one failure does not lead to compromise.

concepts.title: Authorisation to test
concepts.summary: Security testing is lawful only with the system owner's written permission and a defined scope.

concepts.title: Firewall rule
concepts.summary: An ordered allow or deny decision on source, destination, port and protocol; the first match wins and a default deny ends the list.

concepts.title: Network segmentation
concepts.summary: Splitting a network into zones so a compromised host cannot reach everything.

concepts.title: Exposed service
concepts.summary: A listening port reachable by others; each one is attack surface.

concepts.title: Injection
concepts.summary: Untrusted input is interpreted as code by a database, shell or browser.

concepts.title: Parameterised query
concepts.summary: The query text and the values are sent separately, so a value can never change the query's structure.

concepts.title: Cross-site scripting
concepts.summary: Attacker-controlled script runs in a victim's browser; output encoding and a content security policy reduce it.

concepts.title: Broken access control
concepts.summary: A user can act outside their permissions because the server does not check each request.

concepts.title: Cross-site request forgery
concepts.summary: A malicious site makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request; same-site cookies and tokens stop it.

concepts.title: Server-side request forgery
concepts.summary: The server is tricked into fetching an attacker-chosen URL, often an internal one.

concepts.title: Search space
concepts.summary: The number of possible secrets; for n symbols of an alphabet of size k it is k^n.

concepts.title: Password hashing
concepts.summary: Store a slow, salted hash of each password so a stolen database does not reveal passwords.

concepts.title: Multi-factor authentication
concepts.summary: Combining something known, held and inherent; phishing-resistant factors bind to the real site.

concepts.title: RBAC and ABAC
concepts.summary: Role-based control grants permissions by role; attribute-based control decides from user, resource and context attributes.

concepts.title: Session
concepts.summary: State that links later requests to an authenticated user, through a cookie or token.

concepts.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
concepts.summary: OAuth delegates limited access to an API; OpenID Connect adds a standard way to learn who signed in.

concepts.title: Symmetric encryption
concepts.summary: One shared key encrypts and decrypts; fast, with a key distribution problem.

concepts.title: Cryptographic hash
concepts.summary: A fixed-size fingerprint of data that is easy to compute and infeasible to reverse; SHA-256 yields 256 bits.

concepts.title: Asymmetric cryptography
concepts.summary: A public key and a private key, used for key exchange and for signatures.

concepts.title: TLS
concepts.summary: A protocol giving confidentiality, integrity and server authentication over TCP, using key exchange and then symmetric encryption.

concepts.title: Certificate
concepts.summary: A signed statement binding a public key to a name, issued by a certificate authority.

concepts.title: Chain of trust
concepts.summary: A certificate is trusted when a chain of signatures leads to a root the client already trusts.

concepts.title: CVE and CVSS
concepts.summary: A CVE identifies a public flaw; a CVSS score from 0.0 to 10.0 rates its technical severity.

concepts.title: Prioritisation
concepts.summary: Severity is combined with exposure, exploitation evidence and asset value to choose what to fix first.

concepts.title: Secure development lifecycle
concepts.summary: Threat modelling, code review, dependency and secret scanning and testing run through the build, not only at the end.

concepts.title: Security logging
concepts.summary: Recording authentication, access, changes and errors with time, actor, action and outcome, without secrets, and protecting the logs.

concepts.title: Detection
concepts.summary: Turning logs into alerts by rules, baselines and correlation, tuned to limit false positives.

concepts.title: Dwell time
concepts.summary: The time between an intruder's start and its detection.

concepts.title: Incident lifecycle
concepts.summary: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity (SP 800-61 Rev. 2).

concepts.title: Containment
concepts.summary: Stopping the spread quickly while preserving evidence, before removing the cause.

concepts.title: Post-incident review
concepts.summary: A blameless account of what happened, why, and what changes, with owners and dates.

lessons.title: What security protects

steps.headline: Every security failure breaks at least one of three properties: confidentiality, integrity or availability.

lead.text: The three failures above each damage a different property of the same file. When a stranger reads it, its **confidentiality** is lost, because confidentiality means that only the people who are authorised to see information can see it. When someone changes a delivery address or the amount on an invoice, its **integrity** is lost, since integrity means that information changes only in the ways its owners intend. When ransomware locks every copy, its **availability** is lost, since availability means that the information, and the systems that hold it, can be used when they are needed.
Together the three properties are called the **CIA triad**, and the figure sets each failure beside the property it breaks.

afterFigure.text: None of the three requires an attacker. An email sent with the wrong attachment breaks confidentiality, a script with a bug that overwrites the wrong rows breaks integrity, and a failed disk breaks availability, so security covers accidents, faults and careless insiders as well as intruders. A single incident often breaks more than one property: ransomware that encrypts the files takes away availability first, and if the criminals also copied the data before encrypting it, confidentiality goes with it.

diagram.alt: A triangle with confidentiality at the top, integrity at the lower left and availability at the lower right. In each view one property is highlighted beside the incident that breaks it.
diagram.caption: The same customer file fails in three different ways. Use the buttons to see which property each failure breaks.

reveal.text: The thief changed nothing and blocked nobody, which is why the loss falls on one property only.

steps.headline: Two related ideas support the triad: authentication shows who is acting, and non-repudiation stops them denying it later.

lead.text: The triad speaks of authorised people, which raises the question of how a system knows who someone is. **Authentication** is the process of establishing that a user or a program really is who it claims to be, and a later lesson covers the passwords and tokens that do this. **Non-repudiation** goes a step further, because it means that a person cannot credibly deny having done something, such as approving a payment, when the record shows that they did.

Neither is a fourth corner of the triad, since both are means of enforcing it. A file can be restricted to authorised readers only if the system can tell who is asking, and a record can prove who approved a payment only if no one can alter it afterwards, which makes non-repudiation depend on integrity.

steps.headline: Risk is the chance that a threat will exploit a vulnerability in an asset, weighed against the harm it would do.

lead.text: Four words are used with precise meanings in this field. An **asset** is anything of value that you want to protect, such as the customer file, the server it sits on, or the company's reputation. A **threat** is something that could cause harm to an asset, whether a criminal, a careless employee or a flood, and a **vulnerability** is a weakness that lets a threat succeed, such as a disk that is not encrypted. The figure shows the chain: a threat acts through a vulnerability on an asset.

afterFigure.text: **Risk** combines two questions about that chain: how likely it is to happen, and how much it would cost if it did. A threat with no vulnerability to use poses little risk, and a serious vulnerability in an asset worth nothing poses little either. Because the likelihood can be lowered but never reduced to zero, the realistic aim is a level of risk that the organisation accepts, reached at a cost that is justified, and the next screens show how to put a number on that cost.

diagram.alt: A row of three boxes joined by arrows: a threat acts through a vulnerability on an asset, with a box beneath for the risk.
diagram.caption: Risk describes the whole chain. Use the buttons to see the words and then a worked case.

reveal.text: Cost per incident times incidents per year is the expected loss for a year, and the next screen gives it a name.

steps.headline: Annualised loss expectancy is the cost of one incident multiplied by how many times a year it is expected.

lead.text: A cost can be put on a risk by estimating two numbers. The **single loss expectancy**, or SLE, is what one incident would cost, and the **annual rate of occurrence**, or ARO, is how many times a year you expect it. Their product is the **annualised loss expectancy**, or ALE, so that ALE = SLE × ARO. If a breach would cost $40,000 and is expected twice every four years, the rate is 0.5 a year, and the ALE is 40,000 × 0.5 = $20,000.

afterFigure.text: The figure compares that expected loss with the price of a control. Suppose a $15,000 control, perhaps a year of extra monitoring, cuts the rate from 0.5 to 0.1. The ALE becomes 40,000 × 0.1 = $4,000, a saving of $16,000, and because the control costs $15,000 the net gain is $1,000. A control is worth buying when its saving exceeds its cost, while one that costs more than the loss it prevents needs a separate reason, such as a legal duty, because the numbers alone argue against it. Both inputs are estimates, so the ALE is best used to compare options with one another.

diagram.alt: Two bars of expected yearly cost in dollars. Without a control the annualised loss expectancy is 20,000. With a 15,000 control the remaining loss of 4,000 plus the 15,000 comes to 19,000, which is 1,000 less.
diagram.caption: Expected cost per year with and without the control. Use the buttons to switch.

steps.headline: Decide whether a $9,000 control is worth buying against a breach that costs $120,000 and is expected once every five years.

workedSteps.text: One breach costs $120,000, and one breach in five years is a rate of 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2 a year.
Multiplying the cost by the rate gives the ALE without the control.
The control is expected to cut the rate to 0.05 a year, and the same multiplication gives the ALE with the control.
The saving is the difference between the two ALEs.
Taking the price of the control off the saving gives the net gain.

steps.headline: Change the control to one that costs $2,000 and cuts the rate only from 0.2 to 0.15, and judge it again.

workedSteps.text: The ALE without any control is unchanged at 24,000.
With the weaker control the rate is 0.15, so the ALE is 120,000 × 0.15.
The saving is 24,000 − 18,000 = 6,000. Take off the $2,000 price and work out the net gain in dollars.

reveal.text: The control saves $15,000 but costs $20,000, so someone must name another reason, such as a legal duty, before it is bought.

steps.headline: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework groups security work into six functions, which also give this course its map.

lead.text: Everything in this course falls under one of the six functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, which organisations use to describe what a security programme has to do. **Govern** sets the policies, roles and appetite for risk that the others serve. **Identify** finds the assets and the risks to them, **Protect** puts controls in place, **Detect** notices when something has gone wrong, **Respond** acts on an incident, and **Recover** restores normal service. The figure lists the six and then shows where each is met in the lessons that follow.

afterFigure.text: The Framework first appeared in 2014 with five functions. Version 2.0, published in February 2024, added Govern, which reflects the fact that a decision such as whether to buy a control for a $20,000 loss is made by those who run an organisation and not only by its technical staff. This lesson belongs to Govern and Identify, because it asks what is worth protecting and what losing it would cost.

diagram.alt: Six boxes in two rows: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. One view gives what each does and the other gives the lessons of this course that cover it.

lessons.orientation: Name the three properties security protects, say which one a failure breaks, and use annualised loss to judge whether a control pays for itself.
lessons.nextAction: Draw a data-flow diagram of a small system and use STRIDE to list what could go wrong at each point.

blocks.text: Take a file of customer records and consider the ways it can fail the people it describes. A stranger can read it, someone can alter it by changing a delivery address or the amount on an invoice, or it can become impossible to open, as when ransomware encrypts every copy and the business stops until the files come back. All three are security failures, yet they have little in common beyond the file, and the remedy for one does nothing for the others.

Security work therefore begins by saying which of these failures a control is meant to prevent and what that failure would cost if it happened. Once the failure is named and priced, you can compare any lock, filter or password rule with the loss it removes and decide whether it is worth what it costs.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which of three properties a failure breaks, and to work out whether a control saves more each year than it costs.
intro.whyItMatters: A control that cannot be justified in money is hard to defend to the person who pays for it.

recap.keyIdea: Security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability, and a control is worth buying when the yearly loss it removes exceeds what it costs.

blocks.text: You sorted failures by the property they break: reading by a stranger is a loss of confidentiality, an unauthorised change is a loss of integrity, and an outage is a loss of availability. You then turned risk into money, since multiplying the cost of one incident by its yearly rate gives the annualised loss expectancy, and the difference between the loss before and after a control, less the control's price, shows whether it pays for itself.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes a small system apart on paper and asks, at each point where data crosses a boundary, what could go wrong.

lessons.title: Threat modelling

steps.headline: Threat modelling asks four questions about a design, and it works best on a sketch.

lead.text: Threat modelling is a structured way of finding what could go wrong with a system before it is built or changed. It is usually described by four questions: what are we building, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good enough job? The first is answered with a diagram, the second with a checklist of kinds of threat, the third with a decision about each threat found, and the fourth by checking afterwards that those decisions were carried out and that nothing was missed.

afterFigure.text: A common belief is that this needs a security specialist and a finished product, and the reverse is closer to the truth. It is cheapest on a sketch, because moving a box on a whiteboard costs nothing while moving a database after launch costs weeks, and it is best done by the team that knows how the system works, with a specialist helping where one is available. The rest of this lesson answers the first three questions in turn.

steps.headline: A data-flow diagram shows where data moves, and a trust boundary marks where it moves between different levels of trust.

lead.text: The first question is answered with a **data-flow diagram**, which uses only four kinds of element. An **external entity** is a person or system outside your control, such as the customer's browser, a **process** is code that you run, such as the web server, and a **data store** is anywhere data rests, such as the database. A **data flow** is an arrow showing data moving between them, and in the figure the three flows are numbered: flow 1 carries the customer's login and order to the server, flow 2 carries what the server reads from and saves to the database, and flow 3 carries a request to a payment service to charge a card.

afterFigure.text: Switch to the second view to see the line that matters most. A **trust boundary** is drawn wherever data passes between parts that are trusted to different degrees, or that run with different privileges. Here the server and the database sit inside the company's network, while the browser and the payment service sit outside it, so flows 1 and 3 cross the boundary and flow 2 does not. Boundaries are where attention goes first, because data arriving from the less trusted side may have been written by an attacker, and so it cannot be believed until it has been checked.

diagram.alt: A web shop's data-flow diagram. A customer browser sends login and order requests to a web server, which reads and writes a database and asks a payment service to charge a card. In the second view a dashed boundary around the server and database marks a trust boundary, and the flows to the browser and the payment service cross it.

steps.headline: STRIDE is a checklist of six kinds of threat, and each kind violates one security property.

lead.text: The second question, what can go wrong, is easier to answer with a prompt than with a blank page. **STRIDE** is such a prompt, a name made from the initials of six kinds of threat, and it was developed at Microsoft in the late 1990s. **Spoofing** is pretending to be someone or something else, **tampering** is changing data or code without permission, and **repudiation** is denying an action when nothing can prove otherwise. **Information disclosure** is reading what should stay private, **denial of service** is making a system unavailable, and **elevation of privilege** is gaining rights that were never granted.

afterFigure.text: Each kind violates one of the properties met in the first lesson, which is why the checklist covers the ground well. Spoofing violates authentication, tampering violates integrity, repudiation violates non-repudiation, information disclosure violates confidentiality, denial of service violates availability, and elevation of privilege violates **authorisation**, the rules about what each user is allowed to do. STRIDE does not list attacks. It names categories of threat, and a single category can be reached in many ways, so the list tells you what to ask and leaves the answers to the system in front of you.

steps.headline: List the threats to flow 1, from the browser to the server, and choose a response to each.

workedSteps.text: Spoofing comes first. The server receives requests that claim to come from a customer, so ask whether someone could send them while posing as another customer. A guessed or stolen password would allow it, and the response is stronger authentication.

Tampering comes next. The flow crosses the open internet, where a device on the path could change an order before it arrives, so the response is an encrypted connection that also detects changes, which the lesson on TLS covers.
Denial of service asks whether the flow could be flooded until real customers are shut out, and the usual response is a limit on how many requests one source may send.

The remaining three follow the same pattern. The encrypted connection also answers information disclosure, a log of who placed each order answers repudiation, and a check on the server of what each signed-in user may do answers elevation of privilege.

steps.headline: Apply the same questions to flow 3, from the server to the payment service, which also crosses the boundary.

workedSteps.text: Spoofing asks whether the server could be tricked into sending card details to something that only pretends to be the payment service, so the response is to check the service's identity on every connection.
Information disclosure asks whether card details could be read on the way, and the response is again an encrypted connection.
Changing the amount to be charged while the request is on its way is the third kind of threat to review here. Name it.

lead.text: The third of the four questions asks what you will do about each threat that you find.

reveal.text: The next screen describes the four responses, and why accepting needs a written reason.

steps.headline: Each threat gets a decision, to remove it, reduce it, transfer it or accept it, and the decision is recorded.

lead.text: A **mitigation** is a design change or control chosen to deal with a threat, and there are four kinds of response. You can **remove** the threat by removing what it targets, **reduce** it with a control that makes it less likely or less harmful, **transfer** it by making someone else carry the cost, as insurance or a hosted service does, or **accept** it knowingly. The figure applies all four to one threat, a guessed password on the shop's admin page.

afterFigure.text: Accepting is a decision, which is different from overlooking a threat, so it needs a recorded reason, the person who agreed to it and a date on which it will be reviewed. Not every threat has to be fixed, and the annualised loss comparison from the first lesson is one way of judging which are worth fixing. The fourth question closes the loop: when the design changes, with a new feature, a new third-party service or a new boundary, the diagram is updated and the questions are asked again, since a model of last year's system says little about this year's.

lessons.orientation: Draw a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries, list the threats to a flow with STRIDE, and choose a response to each.
lessons.nextAction: Follow an attack from the first look at a target to the damage, and place a defence at each stage.

blocks.text: A web shop has a login page, an order form and a database, and a sketch of those three things on a whiteboard is enough to show where an attacker would go first. The customer's browser is outside the shop's control, so anything it sends could have been written by someone else, while the database sits on a private network and answers only the server. A fault found at this stage costs a conversation to repair, whereas the same fault found after release costs a patch, an outage and perhaps a notice to every customer.
Threat modelling is the habit of examining that sketch systematically, with a diagram that shows where data moves and a checklist of six kinds of threat to apply to each movement.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to draw a small system with its trust boundaries, ask six questions about each flow that crosses one, and record what you decide to do.
intro.whyItMatters: Finding a design fault on a sketch costs an hour, and finding it in production costs far more.

recap.keyIdea: Draw the system, mark the trust boundaries, ask the six STRIDE questions of every flow that crosses one, and record the response to each threat.

blocks.text: A data-flow diagram shows where data moves between external entities, processes and data stores, and a trust boundary marks where it passes between parts trusted to different degrees. STRIDE gives six questions to ask of each flow that crosses one, and each question corresponds to a property from the first lesson, so every threat found can be answered by removing it, reducing it, transferring it or accepting it with a recorded reason.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the attacker's side and follows an attack from the first look at a target to its damage, with a defence placed at each stage.

lessons.title: How attacks proceed and how to layer defences

steps.headline: An intrusion usually passes through seven stages, and each stage is a chance to stop or notice it.

lead.text: Intrusions differ in detail, but most follow the same sequence, and naming it lets a defender ask at each point what could have been caught. It begins with **reconnaissance**, in which the attacker learns about the target, such as staff names and the format of email addresses. **Initial access** is the first foothold, perhaps a password obtained by a phishing email, and **execution** is the running of the attacker's own code on a machine there. **Persistence** lets the attacker keep access after a restart or a password change, **privilege escalation** gains higher rights such as an administrator's, and **lateral movement** reaches other systems from the first. **Impact** is the harm itself: data stolen, files encrypted or a service stopped.

afterFigure.text: The second view of the figure follows one phishing intrusion through the seven stages. The order is a guide, since attackers skip stages, repeat them and run several together, but it is useful because every stage before the last is a point at which no harm has yet been done. A defender who notices unusual activity at lateral movement has caught the intrusion with the damage still to come.

reveal.text: Each stage leaves its own evidence, and a defender can look for it.

steps.headline: Most intrusions use stolen passwords and known flaws, and ATT&CK catalogues what attackers have really been seen doing.

lead.text: It is tempting to picture an attacker with a secret exploit that nobody has seen before, but such tools are rare and expensive. Many intrusions begin far more simply, with a stolen or reused password, or with a flaw that was already public and had a fix that nobody had applied. This matters for defence, because it means that careful basics, such as unique passwords with a second factor and prompt patching, close the doors that are used most often.

afterFigure.text: The organisation MITRE records what attackers have been observed doing in a public knowledge base called **ATT&CK**. It groups behaviour by goal, and a goal such as gaining initial access or moving laterally is called a **tactic**, while each particular way of reaching it, such as sending a phishing email, is a **technique**. The seven stages above are a simplification of ATT&CK's tactics, which number fourteen for enterprise systems. Defenders use it as a shared vocabulary and as a checklist: for each technique, is there a control that prevents it, and a log that would show it?

reveal.text: The next screen explains why the controls multiply in this way, and what the layers are.

steps.headline: Defence in depth places several independent controls in the path, so that one failure does not mean a breach.

lead.text: No control stops everything: patches arrive late, people are deceived and rules are misconfigured. **Defence in depth** therefore stacks controls so that an attacker who defeats one meets another. For a customer database the layers run from the outside in. A **network** layer keeps the database on its own segment where only the application server can reach it, a **host** layer keeps the server patched and its software limited to what it needs, and an **application** layer requires every user to sign in and checks what they may do. An **identity** layer adds strong credentials with a second factor, and a **data** layer encrypts what is stored. **Detection** runs alongside all of them, with logs and alerts that show when a layer has been tested or passed.

afterFigure.text: Switch the figure to see a layer fail. A failed ring leaves the others in place, so the attacker still has to get through them, and alerts from detection can bring a defender in before the last ring is reached. The layers help only when they fail for different reasons, because two controls that both depend on the same password fail together, and the second then adds little. Since each layer sees only what the one before let through, the share of attacks that passes all of them is the product of the shares that pass each, which the next screens put numbers on.

steps.headline: Work out what share of attacks passes three layers that stop 90%, 70% and 80% of what reaches them.

workedSteps.text: A layer that stops 90% of the attacks reaching it lets 10% through, which is 0.1 as a fraction. The host layer, which stops 70%, lets 0.3 through, and the application layer, which stops 80%, lets 0.2 through.
To combine the three, look at what each layer receives.
Multiplying gives the fraction that gets through all three, and as a percentage it is 0.6%.
No single layer lets less than 10% through, and together the three let through 0.6%.

steps.headline: Add a fourth layer, encryption of the stored data, that stops 50% of what reaches it.

workedSteps.text: The fourth layer lets 0.5 of the attacks reaching it through.
The earlier three layers let 0.006 through, so all four let through 0.006 × 0.5. Give that as a percentage.

steps.headline: Security testing is lawful only with the owner's written permission and a defined scope.

lead.text: Describing attacks lets a defender recognise them, and testing your own defences is how you find out whether they work, yet testing is lawful only with the permission of the system's owner. Laws such as the UK's Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act make unauthorised access an offence, and good intentions do not change that. Scanning a network you do not own is therefore not harmless, even when the scan finds nothing.

Professional testers work from a written agreement that names the systems in scope, the dates and the methods allowed, and they stop at its edge. NIST's guide to security testing, SP 800-115, treats this planning as part of the test itself. For practice, use machines that you own, virtual machines that you build for the purpose, and platforms that are made for it, such as capture-the-flag games and training labs, where the owner has invited the attempt.

reveal.text: A missed patch removes one factor from the product, and the remaining layers carry the whole load.

lessons.orientation: Put the stages of an intrusion in order, place layered controls against them, and say what makes security testing lawful.
lessons.reviewLabel: How attacks proceed and how to layer defences
lessons.nextAction: Scan and read a network the way a defender does, and write firewall rules that allow only what a service needs.

blocks.text: Many intrusions begin with a phishing email. It appears to come from the IT department, its link leads to a page that asks for a password, and once an employee has typed one in, a stranger holds the first thing needed to enter the company's systems. In the days that follow the stranger may read files, copy the customer list and encrypt the servers, and at no point does anything need to be broken, because each step uses a permission that already exists.

Set out in order, the steps of an intrusion become a list of places where a defender can step in, since every step before the last can be noticed and stopped before any harm is done. The order also shows where a control, or several controls in a row, can be placed across the attacker's path, and how to estimate what each one adds.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the stages of an intrusion in order, estimate how layered controls reduce an attacker's chances, and say what permission a test requires.
intro.whyItMatters: Every stage of an attack that you can catch is damage that has not yet happened.

recap.keyIdea: An intrusion passes through stages, and independent layers of controls multiply together to make passing all of them unlikely.

blocks.text: An intrusion usually runs from reconnaissance and initial access through execution, persistence, privilege escalation and lateral movement to impact, and many such intrusions begin with a stolen password or an unpatched known flaw. Defence in depth places independent controls in the path, so that the share of attacks passing all of them is the product of the shares passing each, and testing those controls is lawful only with the owner's written permission and a stated scope.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the network layer in detail: what a scan shows a defender, and how a firewall rule set decides what may pass.

lessons.title: Network security

steps.headline: A port scan lists the services that answer on a machine, and each service that others can reach is part of its attack surface.

lead.text: A port is a number that tells a machine which program should receive incoming data, and a program that waits for connections on a port is called a **service**. A scan lists the ports it tried and gives each a **state**: *open* when a service answered, *closed* when the machine refused the connection, and *filtered* when nothing came back, usually because a firewall dropped the request. Some numbers are worth knowing by sight: 22 for ssh, which gives remote command access, 80 and 443 for web traffic, 445 for Windows file sharing, 3389 for remote desktop, and 3306 and 5432 for the MySQL and PostgreSQL databases.

afterFigure.text: Every service that other machines can reach is part of the **attack surface**, the set of places where an attacker could begin. That is different from saying that an open port is a vulnerable one, since the risk depends on what the service is, whether it needs to be reachable from where it sits, and whether it is patched. The second view of the figure applies this to the scan: the web ports are expected, ssh should be restricted to administrators' addresses, and the database on 3306 should answer only the web server, which makes it the one to take off the internet-facing side.

diagram.alt: A port scan result with five rows: 22 ssh open, 80 http open, 443 https open, 445 filtered, and 3306 mysql open. The second view adds a verdict for each row, marking 3306 as the service that should not face the internet.
diagram.caption: A scan of a public web server. Use the buttons to add a verdict on each line.

reveal.text: A scan states what answers, and judging what should answer is the defender's job.

steps.headline: A firewall checks a packet against its rules in order, and the first rule that matches decides what happens to it.

lead.text: A **firewall rule** is an instruction to allow or deny traffic, stated in terms of the protocol and port, the source and the destination. A firewall holds a list of such rules and checks each packet against them from the top, and the first rule that matches decides the packet's fate while the rules below it are never consulted. The figure uses a small rule set for a web shop: rule 1 allows tcp port 443 from any host to the web server, rule 2 allows tcp port 5432 from the web server to the database, and rule 3 denies everything.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the three packets to follow them down the list. A request from the internet to the web server on port 443 matches rule 1 and is allowed. The web server's query to the database on 5432 fails rule 1, because the destination is wrong, and matches rule 2. A packet from any other host to the database on 5432 matches neither, since only the web server may send it, so it reaches rule 3 and is denied. Because the order decides the outcome, a broad rule placed above a narrow one hides the narrow one, and a rule list has to be read as carefully as program code.

diagram.alt: A firewall rule table with three rules: allow tcp 443 from any to web, allow tcp 5432 from web to db, and deny all. Three views follow a different packet down the list, and the first matching rule is highlighted.

reveal.text: The deny was written to stop strangers, and it stops the web server too, because the order made it the first match.

steps.headline: A rule set ends with deny all, and zones limit how far a compromised machine can reach.

lead.text: The last rule of the set above, which denies everything, is called **default deny**. It reverses the burden of proof, so that traffic is blocked unless a rule has been written to allow it, and a forgotten rule then causes an outage that someone notices and fixes, where the opposite default would cause an exposure that nobody notices. A set that ends in an allow-all rule gives little protection, since every earlier deny would have to foresee every unwanted packet.

A firewall at the edge of a network does not protect what is already inside it. Attackers often arrive from within, through a phished laptop or a stolen password, and on a flat network where every machine can reach every other, that first foothold can reach the database directly. **Network segmentation** splits the network into zones, such as one for users, one for servers, one for databases and one for guests, with a firewall and a default deny rule between them. Each flow that a zone needs is allowed by name, and the rest, including the route from a user's laptop to the database, is blocked.

afterFigure.text: In the second view the same phished laptop can reach only what the user zone is allowed to reach. Segmentation also turns lateral movement, the stage met in the last lesson, into a series of blocked steps that the firewall's logs can record, and a separate guest zone keeps visitors' devices away from everything else.

steps.headline: Write the rule set for a web shop. Customers reach the web server, the web server reaches the database, and administrators sign in over ssh from the office.

workedSteps.text: List each flow that must work and name its source, destination and port: customers to the web server on tcp 443, the web server to the database on tcp 5432, and the office network to the web server on tcp 22.
workedSteps.math: 443: any to web. 5432: web to db. 22: office to web.

workedSteps.text: Write one allow rule for each flow, with the narrowest source that works.
End the list with a rule that denies everything else.

Trace a packet from the internet to the database on tcp 5432. Rule 1 names the wrong port and destination, rule 2 allows only the web server as source, and rule 3 names the wrong port, so rule 4 decides.

steps.headline: Trace a packet from a host on the internet to the web server on tcp 22.

workedSteps.text: Rule 1 is about tcp 443, so it does not match.
Rule 2 is about the database, so it does not match either.
Rule 3 names port 22 and the web server, but only for sources in the office network, and this host is outside it, so it does not match.
Give the number of the rule that decides the packet.

steps.headline: WPA2 or WPA3 with a long passphrase protects a wireless network, while hiding its name or filtering addresses does not.

lead.text: A wireless network broadcasts to anyone in range, so its protection has to come from encryption. The oldest scheme, WEP, was shown in 2001 to be breakable by someone who collects enough traffic, and it was replaced by WPA and then by **WPA2**, ratified in 2004. **WPA3**, announced in 2018, strengthens the way a device proves that it knows the passphrase, so that a recorded exchange cannot be tested against guesses at leisure. WPA2 or WPA3 with a long, unique passphrase is the right default for a home or a small office.

afterFigure.text: Two popular measures add little. Hiding the network name does not hide the network, because the name is sent in the frames that devices exchange whenever they connect, and filtering by hardware address fails because addresses can be read from the air and copied. Another thing to understand is the **deauthentication** attack, in which forged messages make devices disconnect. It can cut a connection, which affects availability, but it does not reveal the passphrase or the traffic, and the protected management frames of WPA3 make it harder still.

reveal.text: The two measures that look like security were never encryption, so the protocol is the one thing that changes the outcome.

lessons.orientation: Read a port scan and a firewall rule set, and choose zones and wireless settings that limit what an attacker can reach.
lessons.nextAction: See how attackers abuse a web application that trusts its input, and how to write queries and pages that cannot be tricked.

blocks.text: A server's owner scans their own machine and receives a short list: port 22 open, port 80 open, port 443 open, port 3306 open. Each line names a program that is waiting for connections, and each of those programs can be reached by anyone whose network can reach the machine. Some of the four are meant to be public, since a web server has to answer on 80 and 443, but one is a database that should answer only the web server beside it, and nothing in the list says whether it does.

Read alongside the firewall's rules, a list like this tells you which programs on a machine anyone can reach and which only the machines that need them can reach. With both in front of you, you can say which service should come off the internet-facing side, follow any packet down a rule list to the rule that decides it, and see how dividing a network into zones limits what a single compromised laptop can touch.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which services in a scan should not face the internet, work out which rule in a list decides a packet, and name the wireless settings that matter.
intro.whyItMatters: Most network attacks reach only what the rules and zones let them reach, so the rules and zones are worth reading carefully.

recap.keyIdea: A firewall's first matching rule decides each packet, so a rule set should end in default deny, and zones keep a compromised machine from reaching everything.

blocks.text: A scan shows which services answer on a machine, and each reachable service is attack surface whether or not it is vulnerable. A firewall reads its rules from the top and obeys the first that matches, so order matters and the list should end with default deny, while segmentation limits how far a phished laptop can reach, and a wireless network is protected by WPA2 or WPA3 and a long passphrase rather than a hidden name.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves up to the web application, where a site that trusts what it receives can be made to run an attacker's instructions.

lessons.title: Injection and cross-site scripting

steps.headline: A program that builds a query by joining text hands the database a single string, and the database cannot tell whose words are whose.

lead.text: Many programs build a database query by joining pieces of text. The programmer writes the start of the query, SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = ', the program adds whatever the visitor typed, and then it closes the quote. The figure follows two honest names through this process: with Ada typed, the database receives a query about Ada and returns her row.

afterFigure.text: The important detail is what the database receives, which is the final joined text and nothing else. It parses that text from left to right, deciding where the quotes open and close, and it has no record of which characters came from the programmer and which from the visitor. Everything depends on the visitor's text behaving like a name, and the program has done nothing to make sure that it does. The next screen asks what happens when it does not.

diagram.alt: A query built by joining program text to typed input. The input Ada is placed between quotes, and the database receives a query for Ada and returns one row of a three-row users table.
diagram.caption: A query built by joining text. Use the buttons to try two honest names.

reveal.text: The visitor's quotes closed the string early and the rest became part of the query, which the next screen names.

steps.headline: Injection happens when input is read as code, and a parameterised query prevents it by sending the values apart from the query text.

lead.text: The fault lies in building one string from two kinds of material: the programmer's own query text, which should be code, and the visitor's input, which should be only data. The database sees the combined text, so a quote typed by a visitor is read as part of the query's syntax. This pattern is called **injection**, since untrusted input is read as code by a database, an operating system shell or a browser, and the query above is a case of **SQL injection**.

A **parameterised query** removes the confusion by sending the two kinds of material separately. The query text carries a marker for each value, as in WHERE name = ?, and the database parses the query before any value arrives. The value is then supplied on its own channel and is treated as a value whatever characters it contains, so a quote inside it is only a quote.

afterFigure.text: Escaping quotes by hand is not an equivalent fix. It depends on knowing every character that is special in every context, and one missed case reopens the hole, whereas parameters remove the possibility itself. Input validation, such as rejecting a name longer than fifty characters, is useful as a second layer, but the control sits where the data is used. The same pattern holds for operating system commands: pass arguments to a program as a list, and do not assemble them into one command string.

diagram.alt: Two ways of sending a query and a typed value to a database. Joined into one string, the typed text is read as part of the query. Sent separately as a parameter, it is treated only as data.

reveal.text: The query's structure is settled before any value arrives, and that is what makes a parameter safe.

steps.headline: A login query is built from two typed values. Work out how many of the 4 rows come back when the password field holds a quote, the word OR and the text '1'='1.

workedSteps.text: The program builds the text SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'Ada' AND password = '' OR '1'='1'; the visitor typed Ada as the name and ' OR '1'='1 as the password, and the program's own final quote closes the last string.
Before testing a row, group the condition as the database does. One of the operators AND and OR binds more tightly, and that operator groups first.
For each row the bracketed part is false, since no stored password is empty, but '1' = '1' is true whichever row is being tested.
A condition that is true for every row returns every row, and a login check that accepts any returned row lets the visitor in.

steps.headline: Send the same two values as parameters instead, and see what the database returns.

workedSteps.text: The query text is sent first with markers for the values, and the database parses it before it sees any value.
The values arrive separately, Ada and the text ' OR '1'='1, and the database compares each with a stored value as plain text.
Now count the rows whose stored password equals that whole text.

steps.headline: Cross-site scripting happens when a page puts attacker-controlled text into its HTML unencoded, and the cure is to encode it for the place where it lands.

lead.text: The same pattern appears in the browser. Suppose a comment page builds each comment into its HTML by inserting the visitor's text between tags. If a visitor submits a comment that contains a script, the page delivers it to every later reader as part of the page, and each reader's browser, which cannot tell the site's code from the comment, runs it. This is **cross-site scripting**, or **XSS**. When the script is saved on the server and sent to every visitor it is called *stored* XSS, and when it is reflected from a request into the response it is called *reflected* XSS.

The script runs with the site's own authority, so it can do whatever the reader could do: read what the page shows, act on the reader's behalf and, unless the cookie is protected, read the session cookie and let the attacker become the reader. The pop-up alert used in demonstrations only shows that a script ran.

afterFigure.text: The defence is **output encoding**, which turns the characters that mean something to HTML into harmless text before the input is inserted. The less-than sign becomes <, for example, so that a script tag is displayed as letters and never run. The right encoding depends on where the text lands, because an HTML body, an attribute, a JavaScript string and a URL each have their own special characters, which is why the rule is called context-aware encoding and why modern template engines apply it by default. A **Content Security Policy**, a header that tells the browser which scripts it may run, adds a second layer that limits the damage if an encoding is missed.

diagram.alt: A comment containing a script tag passes through a page template to a reader's browser. Without encoding the browser runs the script, and with output encoding it shows the text.

lessons.orientation: Explain why joining input into a query or a page is dangerous, and fix it with parameters and output encoding.
lessons.nextAction: See how a site decides who may do what, and how requests can be forged when it decides carelessly.

blocks.text: Behind many login forms a line of code builds a database query by joining two pieces of text: the programmer's own query, SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = ', and whatever the visitor typed into the form, followed by a closing quote. When the visitor types Ada, the database receives a query about Ada. The database never sees the two pieces separately, however, only the joined text, so a visitor who types something that contains a quote has written part of the query.

Text written by a stranger and placed inside code that a machine will run is the mistake behind both SQL injection and cross-site scripting, two of the oldest faults on the web, which have been listed among the OWASP Top 10 risks for many years. Following the visitor's text to the place where it lands lets you say what such a query or page will do, and the fixes, parameters for a database and encoding for a page, follow from keeping the two kinds of text apart.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict what an injected query returns, fix SQL injection with parameters and cross-site scripting with output encoding.
intro.whyItMatters: These two faults are common and old, and the fixes are mechanical once you can see where code and data are mixed.

recap.keyIdea: Injection happens when input is read as code, and the fix is to keep data apart from code, with parameters for queries and encoding for pages.

blocks.text: A query or a page built by joining text gives the interpreter one string, so it cannot tell the programmer's code from the visitor's data, and a quote or a tag in the input becomes part of the code. A parameterised query sends values on a separate channel, and output encoding turns the characters that matter to HTML into plain text, so in each case the input stays data.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from what a page does with input to who is allowed to see what, and how a forged request can borrow a signed-in user's rights.

lessons.title: Broken access control and forged requests

steps.headline: Broken access control means that the server does not check, on every request, that this user may act on this object.

lead.text: The example above is a **broken access control**: a user can act outside their permissions because the server does not check each request. Its common form is the **insecure direct object reference**, in which an identifier in the request, such as the invoice number in /invoices/1042, names an object directly and the server fetches whatever it names. Signing in proves who the user is, which is authentication, but it says nothing about which invoices that user may see. That second question, authorisation, has to be answered separately, for each request and each object.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets four requests beside the user who sent each and the people allowed to see the object, and the second view marks the decision that a correct server makes. Three beliefs lead people to skip the check. Hiding a link or a button does not protect the page behind it, because a user can type the address. Making identifiers long and random only makes the flaw harder to find, and leaves the object open to anyone who learns the identifier from a shared link or a log. Checking only when a page first loads fails when the same data is fetched again by another route. The rule is that **the server decides, on every request, for every object**.

diagram.alt: A table of four requests with the signed-in user, the request, and who may see the object. User 7 requests invoice 1042 which is theirs, invoice 1043 which belongs to user 9, and an admin page for staff. User 9 requests invoice 1043. The second view marks which are allowed and which denied.

request.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The server never has to guess who is asking, only to compare the signed-in user with the object on each request.

steps.headline: Cross-site request forgery abuses the browser's habit of attaching cookies automatically, and tokens and SameSite cookies stop it.

lead.text: A browser attaches the cookies it holds for a site to the requests it sends to that site, and it does so whichever page caused the request. That keeps a user signed in, but it has a consequence. Suppose a user is signed in to a bank and, in another tab, opens a page run by someone else. That page can contain a hidden form that sends a transfer request to the bank, and the browser will attach the bank's session cookie to it. The bank receives a request with a valid cookie and has no way of knowing that the user never asked for it. This is **cross-site request forgery**, or **CSRF**, and it works for actions only, since the attacking page cannot read the bank's reply.

afterFigure.text: Using POST instead of GET does not help, because a hidden form can submit a POST as easily, and the browser attaches the cookie either way. Two defences work. A **CSRF token** is a random value that the server places in its own forms and checks when they come back, and a page on another site cannot read it, so it cannot include it. The **SameSite** cookie attribute tells the browser not to attach the cookie to requests that begin on another site. Recent browsers treat a cookie without the attribute as Lax, which withholds it from most cross-site requests, but a site should set it explicitly, because the default is not universal and Lax still sends the cookie on a top-level GET navigation, which is why changes must never be made by GET.

diagram.alt: A sequence of requests between another site, the browser and a bank. A normal transfer carries the session cookie because the user pressed Send. In a forged request a hidden form on another site makes the browser send the same transfer with the cookie. With the SameSite attribute the browser leaves the cookie off and the bank rejects it.
diagram.caption: A transfer request in three situations. Use the buttons to compare a normal request, a forged one, and a forged one with SameSite.

reveal.text: The method makes no difference, so the defence has to stop the cookie travelling or require a value that the other site cannot supply.

steps.headline: Server-side request forgery turns a server that fetches addresses into a tool for reaching places that only the server can reach.

lead.text: Some features make the server fetch an address for the user: importing a picture from a link, previewing a web page, checking a webhook. If the address comes from the user and the server fetches it without checking, the user chooses where the server's request goes, and the server sits inside the network and often has more access than the user. This is **server-side request forgery**, or **SSRF**. The targets are internal services that the internet cannot reach, an admin console on the same machine, and, in cloud environments, the instance's metadata service, which hands out credentials to the machine. One example is the link-local address 169.254.169.254, which Amazon Web Services uses for instance metadata.

afterFigure.text: The defence follows from the cause. The server should accept destinations only from an **allowlist** of the hosts the feature needs, because a blocklist of bad addresses misses alternative spellings of the same address and redirects from an allowed host to a blocked one. It should also refuse addresses that resolve to internal ranges, check again before following any redirect, and run with network rules that keep the application away from the metadata address unless it needs it. Cloud providers add their own layer: version 2 of Amazon's metadata service requires a session token, so a simple forwarded request is not enough.

diagram.alt: Three views of a feature in which a web app fetches a link supplied by a user. Used as intended it fetches a public photo. Pointed at an internal metadata service it fetches from inside the network and returns the result. With an allowlist the request is refused.

steps.headline: For each of three suspicious requests, name the flaw and say where the server must check.

workedSteps.text: Request A: user 7 asks for /invoices/1043, which belongs to user 9. The identifier names the object directly, so this is a direct object reference, and the check belongs on the server, which compares the invoice's owner with the signed-in user before returning it.

Request B: a hidden form on another site posts a transfer to the bank, and the browser attaches the user's session cookie. The server cannot tell this from a real request, so the defence is to stop the cookie travelling or to require something the other site cannot supply.
workedSteps.math: B: SameSite cookie or CSRF token

workedSteps.text: Request C: a feature that fetches a picture from a link is given the address of the internal metadata service. The server is being asked to make a request for the visitor, so the check belongs in its outbound code, which compares the destination with an allowlist.
In each case the check is made by the server, in code that the user cannot edit, when the request arrives or is sent.
workedSteps.math: Check on the server, every time

steps.headline: Triage a fourth request. The link to /admin/users is hidden from ordinary users' menus, yet a user who types the address sees the page.

workedSteps.text: The menu hides the link, which changes only what the browser shows.
The address still works, and the server answers because it never checks the user's role.
workedSteps.math: No role check on the server

workedSteps.text: Name the flaw that lets an ordinary user reach the page.

reveal.text: Hard-to-guess identifiers reduce how often the flaw is found, and the ownership check still has to be made.

lessons.orientation: Recognise a changed identifier, a forged cross-site request and a forged server request, and say where the server must check.
lessons.reviewLabel: Broken access control and forged requests
lessons.nextAction: Judge a password scheme by the size of the space an attacker must search, and store passwords so that a leak does not reveal them.

blocks.text: A signed-in customer, user 7, is looking at their invoice at the address /invoices/1042. The number is the invoice's identifier, and nothing prevents the customer from editing it to 1043. If the server returns that invoice, which belongs to someone else, the fault does not lie in the form or in the database query, because the server never asked whether user 7 is allowed to see invoice 1043. Broken access control was ranked first in the 2021 edition of the OWASP Top 10, and a newer edition may reorder the list.

An edited identifier is one way for a request to carry more authority than the person behind it has. A request can also be sent by the victim's own browser at the bidding of another site, or made by the server itself to an address that an attacker supplied, and in each case the defence is a check that the server makes on its own side before it acts. Knowing where that check belongs lets you look at a suspicious request and say which flaw it exploits and what would have stopped it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to recognise each of the three flaws in a request and say which check on the server, in the browser's cookie or in outbound code stops it.
intro.whyItMatters: Each of these flaws is a request that the server accepted without asking who wanted it and for what.

recap.keyIdea: A server must decide on every request who is asking and what they may reach, because hidden links, post methods and obscure identifiers decide nothing.

blocks.text: A changed identifier succeeds when the server fetches the object without comparing its owner with the signed-in user, so the check belongs on the server for every request. A forged cross-site request succeeds because the browser attaches cookies automatically, which a token or a SameSite cookie prevents, and a forged server request succeeds when a server fetches an address it was given, which an allowlist of destinations prevents.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at passwords, the check these flaws sit beside, and asks how large a space an attacker must search and how a leak should be stored against.

lessons.title: Passwords and authentication

steps.headline: The strength of a password against guessing starts from the size of its search space, which is the alphabet size raised to the length.

lead.text: If an attacker knows nothing about a password except which symbols it may contain and how long it is, the number of passwords they might have to try is its **search space**. A password of n symbols, each chosen from an alphabet of k symbols, has k × k × … × k possibilities, written k^n, because each of the n positions can be filled in k ways independently of the others. Letters of both cases and the digits give an alphabet of 62 symbols, so eight characters give 62^8 = 218,340,105,584,896 possible passwords.

afterFigure.text: The count means little until it is set against a guessing speed. At 10 billion guesses a second, trying every one of them takes 218,340,105,584,896 ÷ 10,000,000,000 = 21,834 seconds, which is 6.07 hours, and on average the right password turns up after half of that. The figure shows how the time grows with the length and the alphabet. Length matters far more than the choice of symbols, since each extra character multiplies the time by the alphabet size, while a wider alphabet raises only the base.

diagram.alt: Bars showing how long a full search takes at 10 billion guesses a second. For 8 characters: 26 symbols about 21 seconds, 62 symbols about 6 hours, 94 symbols about 7 days. For 12 characters: 110 days, 10,000 years and 1.5 million years.

reveal.text: Even this space is searched in a fraction of a second at the speed above, which is why short passwords are not defended by their alphabet.
The next screen measures this growth in bits, and asks what a person can do to raise it.

steps.headline: Length and unpredictability add strength, while composition rules and forced changes add little.

lead.text: Security engineers measure the size of a search space in **bits**, where a space of N possibilities is worth log2 N bits and each extra bit doubles it. Eight random characters from 62 are worth 47.6 bits. Four words chosen at random from a list of 7,776 are worth 51.7 bits, since each word contributes log2 7,776 = 12.9 bits, and the four words, called a passphrase, are the harder to guess and much easier to remember. A fifth word would add another 12.9 bits, as the figure shows.

afterFigure.text: The random choice is what counts, and the figures assume it. A name with its first letter capitalised and a digit added at the end has a far smaller search space than 62^8, because people choose from a small set of patterns and attackers try those first. NIST's guidance on digital identity therefore advises against forced composition rules, such as one capital and one symbol, and against changing passwords on a schedule, which pushes people towards predictable changes. It advises allowing long passphrases, checking new passwords against lists of those exposed in breaches, and asking for a change only when there is evidence of compromise. Uniqueness matters as much as length, because a reused password is only as safe as the weakest site that holds it, and attackers try credentials from one breach on other sites, which is called **credential stuffing**.

steps.headline: A site should store a slow, salted hash of each password, so that a stolen database does not reveal the passwords.

lead.text: There are four ways to store passwords, and three of them fail. Plain text exposes every password the moment the database leaks. Encryption with one key fails in the same way, because the application needs the key and a thief often takes it with the database. A **hash** is a one-way function that turns a password into a fixed-length fingerprint which cannot be turned back, and a site that stores only hashes checks a login by hashing the attempt and comparing it with the stored fingerprint. A hash is therefore not the same as encryption, which is reversible by design. Yet a fast hash such as SHA-256 is built for speed, so an attacker holding the stolen hashes can test billions of guesses a second offline.

afterFigure.text: Two additions close the gap. A **salt** is a random value generated for each user and stored beside the hash, and it is mixed into the password before hashing, so that two users with the same password get different hashes and a table of precomputed hashes is useless. A **slow hash** such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 is deliberately expensive to compute, and scrypt and Argon2 also demand a lot of memory, which blunts the advantage of graphics hardware. Each login then takes a fraction of a second, which no user notices, while each guess costs the attacker the same fraction, and the attacker must work on one user at a time.

diagram.alt: Two users, Ada and Grace, who chose the same password. Without a salt both stored hashes are identical. With a random salt for each user the stored hashes differ.

steps.headline: Work out how long a full search takes against 9 characters from lowercase letters and digits, at 10 billion guesses a second.

workedSteps.text: The alphabet has 26 letters and 10 digits, so k = 36, and the password has n = 9 characters.
Each of the 9 positions can be filled in 36 ways, so the search space is 36^9.
Compare it with the space for 8 characters, which is 36^8 = 2,821,109,907,456, and ask what the ninth character does.
Divide the candidates by the guessing speed to get the time in seconds.
Divide by 3,600 seconds in an hour.

steps.headline: Add a tenth character to the same policy, and work out the new time.

workedSteps.text: The space is multiplied by 36 again.
Divide by the guessing speed.
Divide by 3,600 and give the time in hours to two decimal places.

steps.headline: Multi-factor authentication combines different kinds of evidence, and the strongest factors are bound to the real site.

lead.text: Evidence of identity comes in three kinds: something you **know**, such as a password, something you **have**, such as a phone or a security key, and something you **are**, such as a fingerprint. **Multi-factor authentication** asks for two or more kinds, so that a stolen password alone no longer opens the account and the attacker also needs the thing the user holds. Two passwords do not count, because they are the same kind.

afterFigure.text: The factors are not equally strong. A code sent by SMS is better than nothing, but it can be intercepted, or redirected by moving the phone number to another SIM, and NIST classes it as a restricted authenticator. A code from an authenticator app or a hardware key is stronger. Even so, a code typed into a fake site can be passed on to the real one at once, which is how phishing defeats many second factors. **Phishing-resistant** factors, such as a FIDO2 security key or a passkey, close that route, because the key signs a challenge that includes the real site's domain, and a lookalike site on a different domain gets nothing it can use.

reveal.text: A person cannot change a fingerprint after it leaks, which is why it works best beside a factor that can be replaced.

lessons.orientation: Judge a password scheme by the size of its search space, store passwords as slow salted hashes, and say what each kind of second factor adds.
lessons.nextAction: Decide who may do what once a user is signed in, and read the token that carries the decision.

blocks.text: A site stores each user's password as a hash, and an attacker steals the database. Offline, with nothing to slow the attacker down, a rack of graphics cards might test 10 billion guesses a second against a fast hash. At that speed, every password of exactly eight letters and digits, 62^8 = 218,340,105,584,896 of them, can be tried in about six hours. Four words chosen at random from a list of 7,776 give 3,656,158,440,062,976 combinations, which take about four days, although the words are easier to remember than eight random characters.

Figures like these let you judge a password rule by arithmetic, since the number of possible passwords divided by the guessing speed gives the time an attacker needs, and they explain why current advice favours length and random words over forced symbols. They also show that the way a site stores passwords matters as much as the passwords themselves, because a hash that is slow to compute cuts that guessing speed and stretches every one of these times.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute a search space and the time to search it, say how a service should store passwords, and rank second factors.
intro.whyItMatters: A password policy can be judged with a calculator, and the result often differs from what the policy's rules suggest.

recap.keyIdea: Strength against guessing comes from the size of the search space, and a slow salted hash stops a leaked database from handing over the passwords.

blocks.text: The search space of a password is the alphabet size raised to its length, so each extra random character multiplies the work, and random words reach the same strength with less to remember. A site should store a slow salted hash, which cannot be reversed, makes identical passwords differ and makes each guess costly, and a second factor of a different kind, preferably one that is bound to the real site, protects the account when the password is lost.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what a signed-in user may do, and how a session or a token carries that decision from one request to the next.

lessons.title: Authorisation, sessions and tokens

steps.headline: Authentication says who the user is, and authorisation decides what that user may do, by role or by attributes.

lead.text: Signing in is **authentication**, which settles who is asking. What that person may then do is **authorisation**, and it is decided by a model that the system applies on every request. In **role-based access control**, or **RBAC**, each user is given one or more roles, such as editor or viewer, and each role is given a set of permissions, so that Ana, an editor, may edit and read documents while Ben, a viewer, may only read them. The model is easy to explain and to audit, since the question of what Ben may do is answered by looking at one role.

afterFigure.text: Roles struggle when the rule depends on facts about the situation. Take a hospital rule that only a patient's own doctor may read the record, and only while on shift. No role says "doctor of patient 12", and one role for every patient and shift would multiply roles without end. **Attribute-based access control**, or **ABAC**, decides from attributes of the user, the resource and the context, which here are the doctor-patient relationship, the record's patient and the time, and the second view of the figure applies the rule to one request. ABAC is more expressive and harder to audit, because to learn what a user may do you must evaluate the rules over every resource, and many systems use roles for the broad structure and attributes for the exceptions. Whichever model is used, the server applies it on every request, as the last lesson showed.

diagram.alt: Two access models. In role-based control users Ana and Ben have roles Editor and Viewer, and each role carries permissions. In attribute-based control a rule about doctors and shifts is applied to attributes of the user, the resource and the context.
diagram.caption: Two ways of deciding what a user may do. Use the buttons to compare roles with attributes.
