reveal.text: A role describes what kind of person is asking, and an attribute can describe how that person relates to this particular thing.

steps.headline: A session links later requests to a signed-in user through an identifier that the server issues, stores and can cancel.

lead.text: HTTP treats every request as separate, so after a successful sign-in the server issues a **session identifier**, a long random value, and the browser returns it in a cookie with every later request. The server looks the identifier up in its own store to find who is signed in, which means that the identifier is as valuable as the password until the session ends, because whoever holds it is the user. It must therefore come from a cryptographically secure generator and carry at least 64 bits of entropy, so that it cannot be guessed, and the server should issue a fresh one at the moment of sign-in, so that an identifier planted beforehand is worthless.

afterFigure.text: Three cookie attributes protect it. **Secure** makes the browser send the cookie only over HTTPS, **HttpOnly** hides it from scripts running in the page, which limits what a cross-site scripting flaw can steal, and **SameSite**, met in the last lesson, keeps it off requests begun on other sites. A session also needs an end. An idle timeout and an absolute limit bound its lifetime, and logging out must cancel the session on the server, because deleting the cookie in the browser removes only the user's copy and leaves a copy that anyone who recorded it could still use.

reveal.text: The script can still act inside the page, but it cannot take the identifier away and use it from elsewhere.

steps.headline: OAuth lets one application act for a user with limited access, and OpenID Connect adds a standard way of learning who signed in.

lead.text: Suppose a printing service wants to read photos that a user keeps with another service. Asking for the user's password would hand over everything, so **OAuth 2.0** provides a way to grant limited access instead. It names four parties. The **resource owner** is the user, the **client** is the application that wants access, the **authorisation server** signs the user in and issues tokens, and the **resource server** holds the data behind an API. In the authorisation code flow, shown step by step in the figure, the client sends the user to the authorisation server and names the access it wants, called the **scope**. The user signs in there, so the client never sees the password, and agrees, after which the server returns a short-lived code that the client exchanges directly with the server for an **access token** to present to the API.

afterFigure.text: OAuth is a protocol for authorisation, and it does not say who the user is, though it is often used as if it did. **OpenID Connect** is a layer on top of it that adds an **ID token**, a signed statement of who signed in, so that an application can use it for login. Three details keep the flow safe. The code is exchanged over a direct connection and used once, the client proves that it is the one that started the request, with a secret or with PKCE, a one-time secret generated for each request, and the server accepts only redirect addresses registered in advance, so that the code cannot be sent to a lookalike.

diagram.alt: The OAuth 2.0 authorisation code flow with four parties, a user, a client app, an authorisation server and an API. Five numbered arrows: the client sends the user to the authorisation server, the user signs in and agrees, a one-time code returns, the client swaps it for an access token, and the client calls the API with the token.

reveal.text: Keeping issuing and checking apart means that the API never needs to see the user's password or manage sign-in.

steps.headline: A JSON Web Token is signed so that it cannot be altered, but anyone can read it, and the receiver must check more than the signature.

lead.text: Access and ID tokens are often **JSON Web Tokens**, or JWTs. A JWT has three parts separated by two dots, header.payload.signature, and the first two are JSON text written in base64url, which is a way of writing bytes as letters and digits and is not a form of secrecy. Anyone who holds a token can decode the first part, eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9, into {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, and can decode the payload into its **claims**: who the subject is, which service issued the token (iss), which service it is meant for (aud), when it was issued (iat) and when it expires (exp). The third part is the signature, computed over the first two with a key that the issuer holds.

afterFigure.text: The signature gives integrity, because any change to the header or the payload makes it fail, but it gives no secrecy, so a payload must never hold a password or another secret. A receiver therefore makes a series of checks, in the order of the figure. It checks that the algorithm is one it expects, since a token that names the algorithm "none" must be rejected, it verifies the signature, and it checks the issuer, the audience and the expiry. One failed check rejects the token. Because a signed token stays valid until it expires, short lifetimes matter, and cancelling one early needs extra work, such as a list of cancelled tokens.

diagram.alt: A table of the checks a receiver makes on a token: the algorithm, the signature, the issuer, the audience and the expiry. In the first view every check passes and the token is accepted. In the second the expiry has passed and the token is rejected.
diagram.caption: The checks on a token. Use the buttons to move the time from before the expiry to after it.

steps.headline: Read the parts of a token and judge whether the receiver should accept it at 23:30 UTC on 31 December 2029.

workedSteps.text: Split the token at its dots. A signed JWT has the form header.payload.signature, so count the dots that separate the three parts.
Decode the first part from base64url. It reads {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, which is a signing method that the receiver accepts.
Decode the payload to read the claims. The issuer is https://login.example, the audience is shop-api, and the token was issued at 1893452400 and expires at 1893456000.
Compare each claim with what this API expects. The issuer and the audience match, and the time of the check, 1893454200, is earlier than the expiry, 1893456000.
The signature is then verified with the key, and a token that passes every check is accepted.

steps.headline: Judge the same token half an hour after it expires, at 1893457800 seconds.

workedSteps.text: The algorithm, the issuer and the audience are unchanged, so those checks pass.
The expiry check compares the time now with exp, and the token is accepted only if the time is earlier.
Work out by how many seconds the token is past its expiry.

reveal.text: A signed token detects changes. Anything secret needs encryption as well, or must not travel in the token at all.

lessons.orientation: Choose between role-based and attribute-based rules, secure a session, name the parties in OAuth and read a token.
lessons.nextAction: Meet the building blocks of cryptography, and see which of them gives secrecy, integrity or a signature.

blocks.text: HTTP treats each request as a separate message, so a server that has just checked a user's password knows nothing about who sent the next request. To bridge the gap it hands the browser a small piece of data at sign-in, usually in a cookie, and the browser sends it back with every later request. Whoever presents that data is treated as the user, which makes it worth as much as the password, and in larger systems it may also say what the holder is allowed to do and be issued by one service and checked by another.

How that data is issued, protected and checked decides whether a sign-in means anything. Knowing that, you can choose whether a permission rule should depend on a user's role or on facts about the request, set the cookie attributes that keep a session from being stolen, and read a token's contents well enough to decide whether to accept it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose a role or attribute rule, say which cookie attributes protect a session, name the four OAuth parties and read a token's claims.
intro.whyItMatters: Most breaches of identity systems come from a session or a token being accepted when it should not have been.

recap.keyIdea: The server decides what a user may do on each request, a session identifier must be unguessable and cancellable, and a token must be checked as well as signed.

blocks.text: Roles grant permissions by job, while attributes let a rule depend on the user, the resource and the context. A session identifier proves identity from one request to the next and so must be random, protected by Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite, and cancelled on the server at logout. In OAuth the authorisation server issues a token that the client presents to the API, and a JWT is signed to detect change and not to hide its payload, so the receiver also checks its algorithm, issuer, audience and expiry.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson steps back to the tools underneath, hashing, symmetric encryption, public-key encryption and signatures, and asks what each is for.

lessons.title: Cryptography basics

steps.headline: A cipher scrambles a message under a key, and a key space small enough to search offers no protection.

lead.text: According to Suetonius, Julius Caesar protected confidential letters by writing each letter as the one three places later in the alphabet, D for A. Under this rule HELLO becomes KHOOR, and the figure shows the alphabet shifted by a chosen amount. The method has two parts: a general procedure that moves letters along, and a number, the shift, which is called the **key**. A scheme of this kind is a **cipher**, the original text is the **plaintext**, and the scrambled text is the **ciphertext**.

afterFigure.text: Reading a Caesar message needs the key, and a reader who lacks it can only guess. There are just 25 useful shifts, however, so a reader can try them all in a minute and recognise the one that produces words, which makes the cipher worthless against anyone who is trying. Its weakness lies in the size of its **key space**, the number of keys that could have been chosen, and the next screen shows how a modern cipher answers it.

diagram.alt: The alphabet written twice, with the lower row shifted by the key. With a shift of 3, A becomes D, and HELLO becomes KHOOR. With a shift of 7, A becomes H, and HELLO becomes OLSSV.
diagram.caption: A Caesar cipher is the alphabet shifted by the key. Use the buttons to change the shift.

steps.headline: A key space is made safe by its size, and a cipher should stay secure even when everything but the key is public.

lead.text: A key of n bits can take 2^n values, so each extra bit doubles the key space: a 40-bit key has 2^40 = 1,099,511,627,776 values, and a 128-bit key has 2^128, about 3.4 × 10^38. The difference between the two is far greater than it looks. At a billion guesses a second, trying every 40-bit key takes under twenty minutes, while trying every 128-bit key takes more than 10^22 years, so searching all the keys is not how a modern cipher is broken.

afterFigure.text: The Dutch cryptographer Auguste Kerckhoffs stated in 1883 that a system should remain secure even if everything about it except the key is known to the enemy. This is **Kerckhoffs's principle**, and it explains why the best ciphers are public. A key can be changed in a moment if it leaks, whereas a secret algorithm cannot, and an algorithm that has been studied openly for years has survived attacks that a hidden one has never faced. A scheme whose security depends on hiding how it works fails once the method is found, and methods are always found.

reveal.text: Each added bit doubles this time, so a 128-bit key is 2^88 times harder to search than a 40-bit one.

steps.headline: Programs write small ciphers with modular arithmetic and with XOR, and both show why a short key is weak.

lead.text: In code, a Caesar cipher is a loop that moves each letter along by the key and wraps round at the end of the alphabet. The first view of the figure shows it: the function takes each letter's position, with A as 0, adds the key, and takes the remainder after dividing by 26, written % 26, so that Y shifted by 5 wraps round to D. The remainder is what makes the alphabet a circle.

A second small cipher uses **XOR**, written ^ in Python and many other languages. XOR compares two bits and gives 1 when they differ and 0 when they match, so 9 ^ 5 works on 1001 and 0101 bit by bit and gives 1100, which is 12. Doing it again with the same key undoes it, since (9 ^ 5) ^ 5 = 9, so the same operation encrypts and decrypts.

afterFigure.text: XOR is at the core of many strong ciphers, but this small version is weak on its own. If a short key is repeated along a long message, patterns in the plaintext show through in the ciphertext, and a reader who guesses a few letters recovers the key. A key as long as the message, chosen at random and never used twice, is called a one-time pad and cannot be broken, but it is rarely practical because the key must be as long as the message and delivered in secret.

diagram.alt: Three views of a small cipher. One shows a Python function that shifts letters and wraps at 26. The other two show XOR on 4-bit numbers: 9 XOR 5 gives 12, and 12 XOR 5 gives 9 again.
diagram.caption: Two small ciphers. Use the buttons to see the code, then XOR in both directions.

steps.headline: A cryptographic hash is a fixed-size fingerprint of data that is easy to compute and infeasible to reverse.

lead.text: A **cryptographic hash function** takes input of any length and returns a fixed-length fingerprint, called a digest. SHA-256, the function in the figure, always returns 256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal characters since each hexadecimal character stands for 4 bits. The same input always gives the same digest, a small change gives a completely different one, as the second view shows by changing one letter's case, and nobody can work back from a digest to the input except by guessing inputs. A good hash is also **collision resistant**, which means that finding two different inputs with the same digest is infeasible.

afterFigure.text: A hash has no key and hides nothing, so it is not encryption. It is used to detect change, for instance by publishing the digest of a download so that others can compare their own with it, and it is a building block of signatures and of password storage. Hash functions age: collisions were found for MD5 in 2004 and the first for SHA-1 was published in 2017, so neither should be used where an attacker could exploit a collision, and SHA-256 or better is the safe choice. None of this should be confused with an encoding such as base64, which only rewrites bytes as text and which anyone can reverse without a key.

steps.headline: Asymmetric cryptography uses a key pair, and its two main uses are agreeing keys and signing.

lead.text: Symmetric encryption uses one **shared key** to lock and unlock data. It is fast, but the two parties must hold the same secret key before they begin, which is the problem of key distribution. **Asymmetric** cryptography uses a pair of keys, a **public key** that can be given to anyone and a **private key** that its owner never reveals. It has two main uses. In **key exchange**, two parties who have never met combine public values to arrive at the same shared key over an open channel. In a **digital signature**, the owner signs a hash of a message with the private key, and anyone can verify the result with the public key.

afterFigure.text: A signature therefore shows who signed a message and that it has not changed since, because any edit alters the hash. Asymmetric operations are much slower than symmetric ones, so real systems use them briefly, to agree on a shared key or to sign, and then use symmetric encryption for the data itself, which is how TLS works in the next lesson. The figure's first view summarises six primitives and what each is for, including the message authentication code, or MAC, which is a fingerprint made with a shared key so that only a holder of the key can produce it, and the second view shows a signature being made and checked.

steps.headline: Choose a primitive for each of four needs.

workedSteps.text: A service must keep a file's contents secret from anyone who steals the disk. Secrecy for parties who share a key calls for symmetric encryption, such as AES in an authenticated mode.
A site publishes a download and wants users to detect corruption. A fingerprint with no key is enough, so a hash such as SHA-256 is the tool.
A vendor wants users to know that an update really came from the vendor. Only the vendor should be able to produce a valid mark, and users must be able to check it.
A site must store users' passwords so that a stolen database resists offline guessing, which the earlier lesson answered with a slow salted hash.

steps.headline: Choose a primitive for a fifth need.

workedSteps.text: A browser and a server have never met, and they must agree on a key to protect a session.
They cannot send a secret key across the open network unprotected, and a signature or a hash does not create a shared key.
workedSteps.math: not a signature, not a hash

steps.headline: Use vetted libraries and modes, because a cipher is trusted for years of public attack and not for its designer's confidence.

lead.text: Everything above comes with a rule: do not invent your own cryptography, and do not assemble the pieces in ways that nobody has examined. A designer cannot see their own mistakes, and the algorithms in use, such as AES and SHA-256, were chosen after years of open attack by researchers trying to break them. Even with a good cipher the details decide the outcome. Encrypting each block independently, which is called ECB mode, leaks patterns in the data, and reusing a one-time value, a nonce, under the same key can undo the secrecy of a whole stream.

afterFigure.text: The advice is to use a well-reviewed library through an interface that makes the safe choice the default, with an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, which protects secrecy and detects change together. Keys must come from a cryptographically secure random generator, and not from a timestamp or a phrase typed by hand, and they are stored apart from the data they protect. A hidden algorithm earns no credit, in line with Kerckhoffs: the strength of the system lies in the key and in the care taken over everything else.

reveal.text: An encoding hides nothing from anyone who knows its name, and passwords need a slow salted hash instead.

lessons.orientation: Tell symmetric encryption, hashing, signatures and key exchange apart, and say why you do not invent your own.
lessons.nextAction: See how TLS uses these primitives to protect a connection, and read a certificate chain.

blocks.text: According to Suetonius, Julius Caesar protected confidential letters by writing D for A and each following letter three places along, so that HELLO would appear as KHOOR. The scheme fails for two reasons that still organise the whole subject. A reader who learns the rule can read every message, and a reader who does not know it need only try the 25 possible shifts to find the one that yields words.

Modern cryptography answers both weaknesses. It assumes that the enemy knows the method and rests everything on a key, and it makes the number of possible keys so large that trying them all is out of reach.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to run a small cipher by hand, say which primitive suits a need, and explain why published, reviewed algorithms are the safe choice.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong primitive, such as encoding where encryption is needed, is a common and avoidable fault.

recap.keyIdea: Security rests on a key and on published, reviewed algorithms, and each primitive has its own purpose: secrecy, fingerprinting, signing or agreeing keys.

blocks.text: A cipher is safe only when its key space is too large to search and when it stays secure with the method public, which is Kerckhoffs's principle. Symmetric encryption keeps data secret with a shared key, a hash gives a fixed-size fingerprint, and asymmetric keys serve for key exchange and signatures, so the choice of primitive follows the need. Because details such as the mode and the nonce decide the result, you use a vetted library and never your own design.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts these tools together in TLS, which protects most connections on the web, and shows how a certificate chain tells a browser whom it is talking to.

lessons.title: TLS and certificates

steps.headline: TLS gives a connection confidentiality, integrity and a proven server name, and the padlock claims no more than that.

lead.text: **Transport Layer Security**, or **TLS**, is the protocol under HTTPS, and it gives a connection three properties from the first lesson. The data is kept secret from anyone watching the network, which is confidentiality, any change to it on the way is detected, which is integrity, and the client learns that it is talking to the server that owns the name it asked for, which is authentication of the server. The current version is TLS 1.3, published as RFC 8446 in August 2018.

afterFigure.text: The padlock in the address bar reports exactly this and nothing more: the connection is encrypted to the site named in the address. It says nothing about whether the site is honest, since a criminal can obtain a certificate for a lookalike name as easily as anyone else, and a padlock on a phishing page is common. TLS also does not encrypt everything with public keys. Public-key operations are slow, so TLS uses them briefly, to agree on keys and to prove identity, and then protects the data with a fast symmetric cipher, as the last lesson described.

steps.headline: A TLS handshake agrees on keys, proves the server's identity and switches to a fast symmetric cipher in one round trip.

lead.text: The figure follows a TLS 1.3 handshake in five steps. The client begins with a **ClientHello** that lists the algorithms it supports, carries its half of a key exchange, and names the site it wants, shop.example.com. The server answers with a **ServerHello** that chooses an algorithm and carries its own half. From these two halves both sides compute the same secret, which has never crossed the network, and every message after the second is encrypted.

afterFigure.text: The server then sends its certificate together with a signature, made with the private key that matches the certificate's public key, over the handshake so far. Only the real owner of the name can produce it, and this is what authenticates the server. Each side sends a **Finished** message that confirms the whole handshake arrived unaltered, and application data then flows under a symmetric key after one round trip. The key exchange uses fresh temporary keys for every connection, so a server key stolen later cannot decrypt traffic that was recorded earlier, a property called **forward secrecy**.

reveal.text: The expensive public-key steps happen once per connection, and the cheap symmetric cipher does the bulk of the work.

steps.headline: A certificate binds a public key to a name, and a client trusts it when a chain of signatures leads to a root it already holds.

lead.text: A **certificate** is a signed statement that a particular public key belongs to a particular name, such as shop.example.com. It records the name, the public key, the dates between which it is valid and the issuer, and the issuer signs the whole of it with its own private key. The issuer is a **certificate authority**, or CA, an organisation that checks that the applicant controls the name before signing. A browser or operating system ships with a **trust store**, a list of root CAs that it trusts without further proof.

afterFigure.text: Roots rarely sign sites directly, since their keys are kept offline and guarded, so a root signs an intermediate CA and the intermediate signs the site's certificate, called the leaf. The server sends the leaf and the intermediate, and the client checks each signature in turn: the leaf was signed by the intermediate's key, the intermediate was signed by the root's key, and the root is in the trust store. The root's own entry is signed by itself and needs no check, because trusting it is a decision already made. If any link is missing or does not verify, the chain fails and the connection is refused. The figure shows what each of the three certificates records.

reveal.text: Trust starts at the root that the client chose to hold, and each verified signature carries it one link further.
The next screen lists all four checks, and the error code that each failure produces.

steps.headline: Each certificate failure is one failed check, and the error code names it.

lead.text: When a browser receives a chain, it makes four checks, and a failure in any one stops the connection. The **name** in the certificate must match the site that was requested, the **dates** must include today, the **chain** must lead to a root in the trust store, and the certificate must not have been **revoked**, which means withdrawn by its issuer before its end date, for example after a private key was stolen. Each failure has a recognisable code, and the figure sets each one beside its cause.

afterFigure.text: Expiry deserves the most attention in practice, because it is the failure that operators cause themselves. A certificate that is one day late is as unusable as one that is a year late, and a browser rightly refuses it, so services must renew before the date and not after. The industry's rules have been shortening the longest life a public certificate may have, from 398 days to 200 days in March 2026 and to 47 days by 2029, many are already issued for 90 days or less, and automated renewal through the ACME protocol is now common, so that nobody has to remember. A wrong name, an untrusted issuer or a missing intermediate point to a configuration fault on the server, and a revoked certificate is found by asking the issuer. The warning page is never something to click through, because it means that one of the checks standing between the user and an impostor has failed.

steps.headline: Diagnose three connections that fail, using the error that each browser reports.

workedSteps.text: The first browser reports NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID. The certificate's last valid day was 30 May 2026, and the check is made on 2 June 2026, so the dates check has failed. Work out how late it is.

The second reports NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID. The certificate names www.example.com, but the visitor asked for api.example.com, so the name check fails, and the fix is a certificate that lists the api name.
The third reports NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID. The chain ends at a CA that is not in the client's trust store, or the server failed to send its intermediate, so the chain check fails.
In all three cases the browser refuses the connection, since one failed check is enough.

steps.headline: Check how long a certificate valid until 30 May 2026 has left on 20 April 2026.

workedSteps.text: The days left in April after the 20th are 30 − 20.
Add the days of May up to the 30th, which is 30 days.
Give the total number of days remaining.

reveal.text: The checks establish whom you are connected to, and judging whether that party can be trusted is still up to the user.

lessons.orientation: Explain how a TLS connection proves the server's name and protects the data, and diagnose the common certificate failures.
lessons.nextAction: Find and rank vulnerabilities, and build the habits that keep new code from adding them.

blocks.text: A browser that cannot trust a site's certificate stops and shows a full-page warning that carries a code such as NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID, and the code is already a diagnosis: the certificate's dates did not hold. Behind that page lies a short list of checks that every secure connection makes before any data moves, and each check has its own code, so that a failed connection can be read like a failed test.

Those checks are made during the TLS handshake, the short exchange that opens every secure connection, and they rest on certificates, each signed by an authority that the browser already trusts or by one that such an authority has vouched for. Once you know what the handshake does and what a certificate records, a warning page tells you which check failed and why, and the padlock tells you exactly what it does and does not promise.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what each step of a TLS handshake does, trace a certificate chain to its root, and name the check behind each common warning.
intro.whyItMatters: Most certificate trouble is an expiry or a wrong name, and the browser's error code says which.

recap.keyIdea: TLS authenticates the server with a certificate chain, agrees keys by key exchange, and protects the data with a symmetric key, so each warning is one failed check.

blocks.text: A TLS handshake agrees on keys, proves the server's name with a certificate and a signature, and then switches to a fast symmetric cipher, which gives confidentiality, integrity and a named server. A certificate is trusted when a chain of signatures leads to a root in the client's trust store, and a connection fails when the name, the dates, the chain or revocation check does not hold, which the browser's error code states.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes up the weaknesses that sit in the code and software itself, and how to rank them and fix the worst first.

lessons.title: Vulnerabilities and secure development

steps.headline: A CVE names a public flaw, and a CVSS score rates its technical severity from 0.0 to 10.0.

lead.text: A **CVE**, short for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, is an identifier of the form CVE-year-number that everyone uses for the same publicly known flaw, so that a scanner report, a vendor advisory and a news story can all be matched. Each entry records a short description, the products and versions affected, the versions that fix it, and a severity rating. The rating is a **CVSS** score, from the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, which turns a flaw's technical properties into a **base score** from 0.0 to 10.0.

afterFigure.text: The score comes from a short vector of metrics, and the second view of the figure reads one: how the flaw is reached, over a network or only locally, how complex the attack is, whether the attacker needs an account, whether a user has to do something, and how badly confidentiality, integrity and availability are affected. Scores are grouped into qualitative bands: None for 0.0, Low for 0.1 to 3.9, Medium for 4.0 to 6.9, High for 7.0 to 8.9 and Critical for 9.0 to 10.0. The score measures how bad the flaw is in the abstract, and says nothing of how much it matters to you, which is the subject of the next screen.

diagram.alt: Three views of a vulnerability record. The first is an invented CVE entry with an ID, summary, affected and fixed versions, a score of 9.8 Critical and a vector. The second reads the vector metric by metric. The third shows the score bands from Low to Critical with 5.3 and 9.8 marked.

reveal.text: The band tells you how bad the flaw is in the abstract, and ranking a patch queue needs more than that.

steps.headline: Severity is not risk: exposure, evidence of attacks and the value of the asset decide what is fixed first.

lead.text: A team that fixed flaws strictly in order of score would sometimes fix the wrong ones first. Consider a 9.8 on a test server that is cut off from every network, and a 7.5 on an internet-facing web server for which attacks are already being seen. The 9.8 would be severe if anyone could reach it, but no one can, while the 7.5 is reachable by everyone and is being used, so the 7.5 comes first. Three questions adjust the score: can an attacker reach the asset, is the flaw known to be exploited, and what would be lost if it were?

afterFigure.text: Evidence of exploitation is public. CISA publishes a Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue of flaws that have been used in real attacks, and FIRST publishes EPSS, an estimate of the probability that a flaw will be exploited in the next thirty days. Teams combine such signals with the value of their own assets in a rule of their own. The figure's second view applies one example rule: multiply the score by an exposure weight, 3 for internet-facing, 2 for internal and 1 for isolated, and add 10 if attacks have been seen. Real programmes use richer rules, and the point of this one is its shape, which is that reach and evidence move a finding up or down the list.

steps.headline: Security checks belong at every stage of the pipeline, so that flaws are caught near where they are made.

lead.text: A **secure development lifecycle** places checks through the whole path from idea to operation and not only at the end, which is often called *shifting left*, after the diagrams that draw the pipeline from left to right. In design, a threat model like the one in the second lesson finds faults while they cost a conversation to fix. In coding, a reviewer reads each change for security as well as correctness, and a **secret scan** looks for passwords and keys committed by mistake. At build time, **static analysis** reads the source for known dangerous patterns, and a **dependency scan** compares the libraries that the project uses with a database of known flaws.

afterFigure.text: Later stages test the running system by exercising the application with unexpected input in a test environment, and release checks confirm that settings, such as debug modes and default accounts, are safe before anything is deployed. In operation, monitoring and patching continue. The second view of the figure shows why the early stages pay: a key committed by mistake is stopped at the code stage by the secret scan, whereas without it the key reaches operation and must be treated as stolen and replaced. The earlier a flaw is found, the fewer people have seen it and the less has to be undone.

reveal.text: The scan reads the list of libraries and versions, which a lock file or a bill of materials provides.

steps.headline: Developers own their dependencies, scanners need triage, and a clear disclosure channel turns reports into fixes.

lead.text: Patching is not only the work of an IT department. Most modern applications are mostly other people's code, so the team that ships the application owns the flaws in every library it includes, and has to know what it includes. A list of components, called a **software bill of materials**, and lock files that pin versions make that possible. Scanners help, but they find known classes of flaw and they report false positives, so each finding needs triage to confirm that the flaw can be reached in this application, and a clean scan means only that nothing known was found.

afterFigure.text: Sometimes the flaw is found by someone outside, and how the team receives the report matters. In **coordinated disclosure** the finder reports privately, the vendor is given time to fix, and the details are published when a patch exists. A team makes this possible by publishing a **security.txt** file, a plain text file at /.well-known/security.txt that gives a contact address and the disclosure policy, as described in RFC 9116. A finder who sees no way to report may give up, or may publish, and neither helps the users.

steps.headline: Rank five findings with the example rule: score × exposure weight, plus 10 if attacks have been seen.

workedSteps.text: The weights are 3 for internet-facing, 2 for internal and 1 for isolated. Finding B, a 7.5 on an internet-facing server that is being attacked, scores 7.5 × 3 + 10.
Finding E, an 8.1 on an internal database with no attacks seen, scores 8.1 × 2.
Finding A is the 9.8 on an isolated test server, so its weight is 1 and nothing is added.
Findings D and C, the 4.3 on the printer and the 3.1 on the laptop, are both internal, so each is multiplied by 2.
Sorting from the highest priority gives the patch order.

steps.headline: Score a sixth finding, F: a 6.4 on an internet-facing server, with attacks seen.

workedSteps.text: The server is internet-facing, so the weight is 3.
Multiply the score by the weight.
Attacks have been seen, so add 10 to 19.2. Give the priority.

reveal.text: The scanner can test for what it knows, and logic faults, such as a missing ownership check, usually need a person to find them.

lessons.orientation: Read a CVSS severity, rank patches by exposure as well as score, and place security checks in the development process.
lessons.nextAction: Read the logs that record an attack, and judge how quickly a defender notices one.

blocks.text: Tens of thousands of new flaws receive a public identifier and a severity score every year, which is far more than any team can fix at once. A flaw in an upload feature may be recorded as CVE-2026-99999, an invented entry, with a score of 9.8 and a one-line description, and at 9.8 it reads as an emergency. Whether it is one depends on two things that the number does not contain: whether anyone can reach the vulnerable feature, and whether anyone is already using it.

Reading a score together with what it leaves out lets you put a list of findings in the order that removes the most risk first, which is often not the order of their scores. The rest of the work is to let fewer flaws through at all, with checks placed at each stage between a design and a release, where a flaw costs least to fix.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a CVSS score in its band, order a list of findings by exposure and evidence, and name the checks that belong at each stage of delivery.
intro.whyItMatters: A patch queue ordered by score alone puts effort in the wrong place surprisingly often.

recap.keyIdea: A CVSS score rates technical severity only, so patches are ranked by adding exposure and evidence of attacks, and checks are placed through the whole pipeline.

blocks.text: A CVE names a public flaw and its CVSS base score places it in a band from Low to Critical, but the score omits who can reach the system and whether attacks have been seen, which is why a lower score on an exposed system can outrank a higher one on an isolated system. Secure development adds checks at every stage, from threat modelling to dependency and secret scans, and a team that owns its dependencies and publishes a security.txt file can act on reports quickly.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to detection: how the logs that a system keeps show an attack, and how long a defender takes to notice one.

lessons.title: Logging and detection

steps.headline: A security log records who did what, when, from where and with what result, and it must be protected as well as kept.

lead.text: A useful security log entry answers five questions: when it happened, who acted, what they did, where the request came from, and whether it succeeded. The events worth recording are authentication, both successful and failed, access to sensitive data, changes to accounts, permissions and configuration, and errors that suggest someone is probing the system. The first view of the figure shows one well-formed entry. NIST's guide to log management, SP 800-92, stresses that a log is useful only when its entries are complete, consistent and time-stamped from a clock that can be trusted.

afterFigure.text: What to leave out matters as much. A password typed into a failed login, a session token, a card number, or more personal data than the event needs, should never appear in a log, because logs are copied to many systems and read by many people, as the second view shows. More is not better: a log that records everything buries the few entries that matter and costs money to store and search. The log also needs protection, since an attacker who controls a server often edits or deletes its local log to hide the visit. Entries should therefore be sent, as they are written, to a separate log server that the first machine cannot change, with access limited and a retention period fixed in advance.

steps.headline: A log is read as a pattern: a burst of failures from one source, followed by a success, suggests that guessing worked.

lead.text: The figure shows fifteen lines of an authentication log, each with a time, a result, an account and the address of the client. Most lines are ordinary: bob and carol sign in once from their usual addresses. Between 10:01:00 and 10:02:50, however, the same address, 203.0.113.9, fails against the account alice eleven times, about ten seconds apart, and at 10:03:01 the same address succeeds. People do not mistype a password eleven times at that steady rhythm, so the pattern points to automated guessing, and the success at the end suggests that it worked.

afterFigure.text: Reading a log in this way means asking the same few questions of every cluster of lines: is it one account or many, one source or many, a human rhythm or a machine one, and what happened next. The last question matters most. A success after a burst of failures is the moment the incident begins, so the defender looks at what alice's account did from 10:03:01 onwards, such as a changed password, a new mail-forwarding rule or a login to another system, and treats the account as compromised until shown otherwise. The addresses in these examples come from ranges reserved for documentation, so none of them belongs to a real host.

No traveller can do that, which is the idea behind the rule that the next screen names.

steps.headline: Detection rules turn log lines into alerts by counting, comparing and correlating, and each needs tuning.

lead.text: A **detection rule** is a condition over the logs that raises an alert. The simplest is a **threshold**: five failed logins for one account within two minutes. A rule for **impossible travel** compares a user's consecutive logins and alerts when the distance between them, divided by the time, would need a speed that no traveller could reach, which is the arithmetic behind the last question. A rule for a **new administrator** alerts when a privileged account is created, or an ordinary account is given privileges, outside an approved change, since attackers who have gained access often create their own. Rules like these compare events with a **baseline** of normal behaviour, and **correlation** combines sources, for instance a login alert followed within minutes by a large download, which is a stronger signal than either alone.

afterFigure.text: Each rule is a guess about what is abnormal, and guesses are sometimes wrong. A rule that fires on a traveller who really did fly, or on an administrator hired this morning, raises a **false positive**, while one that stays silent during a real attack is a false negative. Tuning narrows a rule until most of its alerts deserve attention, for example by ignoring a known scanner's address or by raising a threshold slightly. Leaving a noisy rule untouched leads to **alert fatigue**: when analysts see hundreds of alerts that come to nothing, they start to close them without reading, and the one real alert is closed with the rest. A smaller set of alerts that each have an owner and a defined response protects better than a larger set that nobody trusts. MITRE ATT&CK lists the techniques seen at each stage of an intrusion, so rules can be written for the stages met in the third lesson.

diagram.alt: Three detection rules. A threshold rule fires on eleven failed logins in under two minutes. An impossible-travel rule fires on logins from London and New York thirty minutes apart. A new-administrator rule fires when an account is made an admin outside a change window.

steps.headline: Dwell time is the gap between an intruder's first action and its detection, and shortening it limits the damage.

lead.text: **Dwell time** is the time from an intruder's first malicious action to the moment that the defender detects it. The figure's timeline follows an intrusion that starts at 09:05, when a staff member opens a phishing link, and is detected at 14:20, which gives a dwell time of 5 hours 15 minutes, or 315 minutes. Defenders track the average across incidents, often as the mean time to detect, as a measure of how well their logging and rules are working.

afterFigure.text: Dwell time matters because the stages from the third lesson take time. Between 09:05 and 14:20 the intruder in the figure establishes persistence, moves to a file server and copies data, and each step comes after the one before it. The second view moves the detection to 09:50, 45 minutes after the start, and the stages after that point never happen. A shorter dwell time therefore means a smaller loss, and every improvement in logging, rules or response speed pays for itself in the way a control did in the first lesson, by reducing the loss from an incident that does occur.

In the second it is detected at 09:50, a dwell time of 45 minutes, and the later events do not happen.

steps.headline: Work out the dwell time for an intrusion that starts at 09:05 and is detected at 14:20 on the same day.

workedSteps.text: Convert each time to minutes after midnight, so that the subtraction takes a single step. 09:05 is 9 × 60 + 5 minutes.
Convert the detection time in the same way. 14:20 is 14 hours and 20 minutes.
Subtract the start from the detection time.
Convert back for the report: 315 minutes is 5 whole hours and 15 minutes over.

steps.headline: Work out the dwell time when the intrusion starts at 22:40 and is detected at 03:10 the next morning.

workedSteps.text: From 22:40 to midnight is 1440 − 1360 minutes.
From midnight to 03:10 is 3 × 60 + 10 minutes.
Add the two parts to get the dwell time in minutes.

reveal.text: The record of the visit has to live where the visitor cannot reach it.

lessons.orientation: Decide what to log, read a short log for an attack, name the main kinds of detection rule, and measure dwell time.
lessons.nextAction: Run the first hour of an incident, from deciding what happened to deciding what to contain.

blocks.text: At 10:03 a user called alice signs in successfully from an address she has never used. A single successful login looks like every other, but the lines before it do not: in the two minutes before, that same address failed eleven times against her account, about ten seconds apart. Read alone, each line says nothing, and read together they say that someone guessed a password and eventually got it right. A log is a record of events, and it becomes a defence when someone, or something, reads it for patterns like this one soon enough to act.

That reading can be done by a rule that watches the logs and raises an alert, so that an intrusion can be noticed while it is still under way, and the time between an intruder's first action and the alert can be measured in minutes. The measure tells a team how well its logging and its rules are working, because every minute an intruder goes unnoticed is time spent on the next stage of the attack.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what an entry should and should not contain, spot a guessing attack in a short log, and compute dwell time in minutes.
intro.whyItMatters: Most intrusions leave a trail in the logs, and detection depends on someone reading it in time.

recap.keyIdea: Log who did what, when, from where and with what result, keep secrets out and copies elsewhere, and judge a defence by how quickly it detects an intruder.

blocks.text: A log entry records when, who, what, from where and the result, leaves out secrets and is sent to a server that the first machine cannot change. Rules such as a threshold, impossible travel and a new administrator turn the lines into alerts, and tuning keeps them few enough to be read. The time between an intruder's first action and its detection is the dwell time, and shortening it stops the later stages of an intrusion from happening.

lessons.title: Incident response

steps.headline: An incident has four phases, and the first begins long before anything goes wrong.

lead.text: NIST's guide to incident handling, SP 800-61, which dates from August 2012 in its second revision, divides the work into four phases. **Preparation** comes first and covers the roles, contact lists, runbooks, logging and tested backups that exist before any incident. **Detection and analysis** confirms that something is wrong, decides how far it extends and how serious it is, and starts the record. **Containment, eradication and recovery** stops the spread, removes the cause and restores normal service. **Post-incident activity** reviews what happened and feeds the answers back into preparation, which is why the figure draws the four as a loop.

afterFigure.text: A common mistake is to think that response starts when an incident does. What decides how the first hour goes is mostly settled beforehand: whether the on-call engineer knows whom to call, whether the runbook says what isolating a server means in this network, and whether the last backup was ever restored in a test. Revision 3 of the guide, issued in 2025, aligns incident response with the functions of the Cybersecurity Framework met in the first lesson, so that it is treated as part of managing cybersecurity risk as a whole.

diagram.alt: Four phases of incident handling in a loop: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, and post-incident activity, with an arrow from the last back to the first. Each view highlights one phase and lists example actions.

steps.headline: Containment stops the spread quickly while keeping the evidence, and the removal of the cause comes after it.

lead.text: Once an incident is confirmed, the priority is to stop it growing. There are three common ways to contain it, each with a different reach. **Isolating a host** cuts it off from the network, which stops it spreading to other machines or sending data out. **Disabling an account** stops anyone using a stolen credential, wherever they are. **Blocking an address** stops traffic to or from a known attacker address, though an attacker can usually change address. The choice depends on what is known, and the figure compares what each one stops and what it leaves open.

afterFigure.text: Containment has a second duty, which is to keep the evidence. A suspected laptop should be isolated from the network and left powered on, since switching it off loses the contents of its memory, which may hold the malicious program and the keys it uses, and wiping it destroys what would show how the attacker got in and what else they touched. Wiping first is a mistake for a further reason, which is that the cause may remain elsewhere, so a clean machine can be infected again within the hour. Containment is followed by **eradication**, which removes the cause, for example by resetting stolen credentials and deleting malicious programs from every host, and then by **recovery**, which restores service from clean backups and watches closely for a return. A restore loses whatever changed since the last backup, so the backup schedule sets how much work can be lost, and every action is written down with its time, so that the team ends with a timeline.

diagram.alt: Three ways to contain an incident: isolating a host, disabling an account and blocking an address. For each, the view shows what it stops, what it leaves open, and what happens to evidence.

reveal.text: Both aims are served together: the spread stops, and what the machine holds is still there for the investigation.

steps.headline: The first hour needs named roles, a running timeline and decisions taken in a stated order.

lead.text: In the first hour of a serious incident, a small team needs defined roles. An **incident commander** makes the decisions and keeps the others from working at cross purposes, a technical lead directs the investigation and the containment, a scribe records every action and finding with its time, and a communications lead handles managers, staff and, where the law requires, regulators and customers. Some laws set deadlines, such as the 72 hours that the European data protection regulation allows, from the moment an organisation becomes aware of a breach of personal data, to notify the supervisory authority, so the time at which the team became aware is itself something to record.

afterFigure.text: The figure compares two first hours that begin with the same alert. In the first, the team confirms the alert, isolates the file server and disables the account in use, then counts the infected machines, and by 03:00 it has three hosts to restore and a record that explains how the attacker got in. In the second, someone wipes the server at once. The wipe removes the evidence of the entry route, the attacker is still inside, and a second host starts encrypting at 02:30. The same effort produces a worse outcome, because the order was wrong: the cleaning came before the containment.

diagram.alt: Two versions of the first hour after the same ransomware alert at 02:00. In the first the team confirms, isolates the server and disables the account, scopes three hosts and has a restore plan by 03:00. In the second someone wipes the server, a second host starts encrypting, and by 03:00 there is no containment and no known entry route.
diagram.caption: The same alert, handled in two ways. Use the buttons to compare the two hours.

reveal.text: A shorter interval between backups loses less work, at the price of storing and testing more of them.

steps.headline: A blameless review asks which controls and processes failed, and ends with changes that have owners and dates.

lead.text: The last phase starts when service is restored, and it is the one most often skipped. A **post-incident review** is a meeting, held within days while memories are fresh, that builds the timeline from the records and asks what happened, why it was possible, what worked and what must change. It is **blameless**: it does not ask who made a mistake, because a person who made a mistake did so inside a system that allowed it, and a team that fears blame hides facts that the next review needs.

afterFigure.text: The output is a short written account and a list of changes, each with an owner and a date: a missing alert gets a new detection rule, a stale contact list gets a monthly check, a backup that took too long to restore gets a faster design. Without owners and dates the list is a wish. The changes then go back into preparation, which closes the loop in the figure, and the measures from the previous lesson, such as dwell time and the time to contain, show over several incidents whether they worked. A good review also records what went well, so that the practices that worked are kept.

steps.headline: Take a ransomware alert through the phases in order, from 02:00 on a shared file server.

workedSteps.text: At 02:00 an alert reports files being renamed with an unfamiliar extension on the server. The first task is detection and analysis: confirm that the alert is real, say which host and which account are involved, and open an incident record with the time.
Once ransomware is confirmed at 02:10, containment comes before cleaning. Isolate the server from the network, leaving it powered on to keep its memory, and disable the account that was used.
Preserve the evidence before anything is changed: copy the logs to the separate log server, capture the memory, and note each action with its time.
Eradication removes the cause. The stolen credential is reset, the malicious program is deleted from every infected host, and the route in is closed.
Recovery restores the service from a clean backup, with monitoring turned up, and returns hosts to the network one at a time.
Afterwards the blameless review records what happened and changes the controls, which feeds the next round of preparation.

steps.headline: Contain a second case: a laptop shows a ransom note, while the other machines look normal.

workedSteps.text: The laptop is confirmed as the affected host, so detection and analysis hands over to containment.
Cutting it from the network stops it spreading, and powering it off would lose its memory.
workedSteps.math: aim: stop the spread, keep the memory

workedSteps.text: Name the action that meets both aims.

reveal.text: Speed matters, and the fastest safe action is isolation, which stops the spread and keeps the evidence.

lessons.orientation: Lead the first hour of an incident through the NIST phases, contain it without losing evidence, and hold a blameless review.
lessons.nextAction: You can now describe how a system is attacked, judge its defences from risk to detection, and run the first hour when one of them fails.

blocks.text: At 02:00 a monitoring system raises an alert: files on a shared server are being renamed with an unfamiliar extension, one every few seconds. The on-call engineer has three questions to answer before anything else, and each is far easier if it was answered earlier: who must be woken, whether the server should be switched off, and where the last good backup is. An incident is the moment at which the quality of earlier preparation is tested, and it is also the moment at which a rushed decision, such as wiping the machine, can destroy what the later investigation needs.

NIST's guide to incident handling, SP 800-61, divides the work into four phases that start long before the alert and end with a review afterwards, and taking them in order is what keeps a team from cleaning a machine before it has stopped the spread. With the phases in mind you can place each action of that first hour, choose between isolating a host, disabling an account and blocking an address, and say how much work a restore from backup will lose.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the phases in order, choose between isolating, disabling and blocking, and write a review that produces changes with owners and dates.
intro.whyItMatters: The first hour's decisions are mostly made in advance, and a clear order of actions protects the evidence.

recap.keyIdea: Prepare before an incident, contain it without destroying evidence, and review it without blame, so that each incident improves the next response.

blocks.text: The lifecycle runs from preparation through detection and analysis and through containment, eradication and recovery to post-incident activity, and the last phase feeds the first. Containment stops the spread by isolating a host, disabling an account or blocking an address, and it keeps the evidence, so a suspect machine is isolated and left powered on and not wiped. A blameless review then turns the timeline into changes with owners and dates.

questions.prompt: A stolen laptop holds an unencrypted customer list, and the thief reads it. The company keeps other copies of the list. Which property of the list has been lost?
hints: Ask what the thief was able to do with the list: read it, change it, or stop others using it.
questions.onCorrect: The thief only read the list, so nothing was changed and the owner can still use it. Only confidentiality is lost.

choices.label: Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the list has been changed, and integrity is lost only when information is altered in a way its owners did not intend.
The company still has its other copies, so the list can still be used when it is needed. The harm is that a stranger has read it.

questions.prompt: A flood of orders crashes a shop's website. Each crash costs the shop $10,000 in lost sales, and crashes happen 3 times a year on average. Roughly what does this cost the shop in an average year?
hints: Each crash costs the same amount.
Think about what three crashes cost together.
questions.onCorrect: One crash costs 10,000 and there are 3 a year, so the yearly cost is 10,000 × 3 = 30,000 dollars, a quantity the next screen names.

choices.label: About $10,000, the cost of a single crash
About $30,000, three times the cost of a crash
About $3,300, the cost of a crash shared over the three

acceptedIdeas: About $30,000, three times the cost of a crash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About $30,000, three times the cost of a crash

misconceptions.feedback: That is what one crash costs, and the shop has three of them in an average year, each costing as much as the first.
Dividing spreads one crash's cost across three, but each of the three crashes costs $10,000 on its own, so the costs add up.

questions.prompt: The control in the example saves $18,000 a year and costs $9,000. Why is it worth buying?
hints: Compare the two yearly figures, the saving and the cost.
questions.onCorrect: The net gain is 18,000 − 9,000 = 9,000 a year, and a positive net gain is the usual test for buying a control.

choices.label: It removes the risk of a breach entirely.
Its yearly saving is larger than its yearly cost.
Spending on security is always justified.

acceptedIdeas: Its yearly saving is larger than its yearly cost.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its yearly saving is larger than its yearly cost.

misconceptions.feedback: The rate falls from 0.2 to 0.05, so a risk of 6,000 a year remains. A control reduces risk without removing it.
Spending has to be justified by what it saves or by another stated duty. A control that costs more than it saves needs a separate reason.

questions.prompt: With the $2,000 control, the ALE falls from 24,000 to 18,000. What is the net gain in dollars after paying for the control?
hints: Find the saving first, the fall in the ALE.
Subtract the cost of the control from that saving.
The saving is 6,000.
questions.onCorrect: A cheaper control that cuts the rate less can still give a positive gain, here 4,000 a year.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the saving before the cost of the control is taken off.
That is the cost of the control, not what is left after paying it.
That is the ALE that remains with the control in place.

questions.prompt: A $20,000 control would cut the rate of a $50,000 loss from 0.4 a year to 0.1. What is the net annual gain in dollars? Give a negative number if the control costs more than it saves.
hints: Work out the ALE before and after the control.
The saving is the difference between them.
Take the cost of the control off the saving.
questions.onCorrect: The control saves 15,000 and costs 20,000, so the numbers argue against it unless some other reason, such as a legal duty, applies.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ALE falls from 50,000 × 0.4 = 20,000 to 50,000 × 0.1 = 5,000, a saving of 15,000. Subtracting the 20,000 cost leaves −5,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the saving. The control costs 20,000, which has to be taken off.
The sign is reversed: the control costs more than it saves, so the result is below zero.
That is the ALE before the control. Compare the saving with the cost.

questions.prompt: An attacker alters the account number on an invoice while it travels between two firms. Which property is broken?
hints: Ask whether the attacker read the invoice, blocked it, or changed it.
questions.onCorrect: An unauthorised change to data in transit breaks integrity, which is why signed or authenticated messages exist.

choices.label: Availability
Confidentiality
Integrity
Non-repudiation

misconceptions.feedback: The invoice still arrives and can be used. Availability concerns whether information can be reached when needed.
The attacker changed the invoice, which is a different failure from reading it. Confidentiality concerns who can read information.
Non-repudiation concerns a person denying an action they took. Here the data itself was altered on its way.

questions.prompt: A loss of $60,000 is expected to occur 0.25 times a year. What is the annualised loss expectancy in dollars?
hints: ALE is the cost of one incident times the yearly rate.
A rate of 0.25 is one incident every four years.
Multiply 60,000 by the rate.
questions.onCorrect: A rate of 0.25 a year is one loss every four years, so the yearly expectation is a quarter of 60,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost of a single loss. The ALE spreads it over the years between losses.
Dividing by 0.25 inflates the figure. The rate multiplies the loss.

questions.prompt: A $5,000 control cuts the rate of a $30,000 loss from 0.4 a year to 0.1. What is the net annual benefit in dollars?
hints: Work out the ALE with and without the control.
Take the control's cost off the saving.
The saving is the fall in the ALE.
questions.onCorrect: A positive net benefit means the control saves more each year than it costs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ALE falls from 30,000 × 0.4 = 12,000 to 30,000 × 0.1 = 3,000, a saving of 9,000. Subtracting the 5,000 cost leaves 4,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the saving. The control's cost of 5,000 still has to come off.
That is the ALE that remains after the control, not the net benefit.

questions.prompt: In the shop diagram, the server and the database sit inside the boundary. Flow 1 goes from the browser to the server, flow 2 from the server to the database, and flow 3 from the server to the payment service. How many of the three flows cross the trust boundary?
hints: Decide for each flow whether its two ends are on the same side of the boundary.
The browser and the payment service are outside the boundary.
Count the flows that have one end inside and one end outside.
questions.onCorrect: Data that crosses a boundary may have been written by someone less trusted, so those flows are examined first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The browser and the payment service are both outside, so flows 1 and 3 cross it. Flow 2 stays inside.

misconceptions.feedback: The server and the database are both inside the boundary, so the flow between them does not cross it.
Both flows that reach outside count, the one to the browser and the one to the payment service.

questions.prompt: An attacker logs in to the shop using another customer's stolen password. Which of the six STRIDE threats is this?
hints: The attacker is pretending to be somebody else.
questions.onCorrect: Using a stolen credential makes the attacker appear to be the customer, which is why authentication is the property at stake.

questions.prompt: A flood of requests could shut real customers out of the shop. Which property of the system does that violate?
hints: The shop could no longer be used when it is needed.
questions.onCorrect: Denial of service is the threat that violates availability, and rate limits are a common response.

questions.prompt: An attacker changes the amount being charged while the request travels to the payment service. Which of the six STRIDE threats is this?
hints: The data is being changed without permission.
questions.onCorrect: Changing data in transit is tampering, and the payment service guards against it by checking that the message arrived unchanged.

questions.prompt: A threat would need physical access to the shop's office and could expose only a public product list, and fixing it would cost more than the list is worth. What is the sensible response?
hints: Compare the cost of a fix with the harm the threat could do.
questions.onCorrect: Accepting is a legitimate decision when the harm is small, as long as the reason and the person who agreed to it are recorded.

choices.label: Reduce it with locks and cameras on the office
Accept it, and record why
Remove it by taking the product list down
Transfer it by insuring against it

misconceptions.feedback: Locks and cameras cost money to protect a list that is already public, so the control would cost more than the harm it prevents.
Taking the list down would remove the threat, but the shop needs its product list to sell anything, so it would lose far more than the threat could cost.
Insurance costs a premium every year, and there is no loss here worth insuring, since the list is already public.

questions.prompt: A message board keeps no record of who posted what, and a user denies posting an abusive message. Which of the six STRIDE threats is this?
hints: The user is denying an action, and the system cannot show otherwise.
questions.onCorrect: The remedy is a log of actions that its users cannot alter, which the lesson on logging returns to.

questions.prompt: An attacker reads customer records that they were never meant to see. Which of the six STRIDE threats is this?
hints: Think about which property is lost when private data is read.
questions.onCorrect: Reading data without permission violates confidentiality, so it is information disclosure.

questions.prompt: Where should trust boundaries be drawn on a data-flow diagram?
hints: Ask what a boundary is meant to show about the two sides.
questions.onCorrect: A boundary marks a change in trust or privilege, and data that crosses it deserves a check.

choices.label: Around every process
Only at the firewall
Wherever data crosses between different levels of trust or privilege
Only around the database

acceptedIdeas: Wherever data crosses between different levels of trust or privilege
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Wherever data crosses between different levels of trust or privilege

misconceptions.feedback: Boundaries mark changes of trust. Two processes that are trusted equally and run with the same privileges need none between them.
A firewall is one place where trust changes, but a boundary is also needed between a server and a third-party service or between user and administrator privileges.
The database is often inside a boundary, but boundaries are drawn wherever trust changes, wherever that is.

questions.prompt: A diagram has 4 flows that cross trust boundaries. The team asks one question per STRIDE category about each of them. How many questions is that?
hints: Count the STRIDE categories.
Each flow is asked about every category.
Multiply the number of flows by the number of categories.
questions.onCorrect: Twenty-four short questions can be worked through in a meeting, which is why the method suits a sketch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 4 flows and 6 categories, and 4 × 6 = 24.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two numbers. Each flow gets all six questions, so the numbers multiply.
That is only the number of flows. Each one is asked about six categories.

questions.prompt: A defender finds a scheduled task that nobody on the team created, set to start a program every night, so that the attacker can return after the machine restarts. Which of the seven stages is this?
hints: The task exists so that access survives a restart.
questions.onCorrect: Persistence mechanisms such as scheduled tasks are a common place to look when cleaning up after an intrusion.

questions.prompt: One control stops 80% of the attacks that reach it, and a second control stops 80% of those that get past the first. Roughly what share of attacks gets past both?
hints: A control that stops 80% lets 20% through.
The second control sees only what the first let through.
questions.onCorrect: Each control lets 20% through, so 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04, or 4% of attacks, get past both.

choices.label: About 20%, the same as with one control
None, since two controls of 80% cover every attack
Much less than 20%, only a few in every hundred

acceptedIdeas: Much less than 20%, only a few in every hundred
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Much less than 20%, only a few in every hundred

misconceptions.feedback: The second control acts on the 20% that passed the first and stops most of those too, so fewer get through than with one control.
The second control sees only the attacks that passed the first, so its 80% is a share of a smaller number, and the two percentages cannot be added.

questions.prompt: Why can the pass fractions of the three layers be combined by multiplying them?
hints: Think about what the host layer receives.
questions.onCorrect: This holds only when the layers fail for different reasons. Two layers that depend on one password fail together.

choices.label: Each layer sees only what the layer before let through.
Every layer stops the same share of attacks.
The strongest layer decides the result and the others add nothing.

acceptedIdeas: Each layer sees only what the layer before let through.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each layer sees only what the layer before let through.

misconceptions.feedback: The layers stop different shares, 90%, 70% and 80%. Multiplication works because each acts on what remains.
Every layer contributes. The combined fraction is smaller than that of the strongest layer alone.

questions.prompt: Adding a layer that stops 50% of what reaches it lets 0.5 through. The earlier three layers let through 0.006 of attacks. What percentage gets past all four?
hints: Multiply the earlier fraction by the new layer's pass fraction.
0.006 × 0.5 gives a fraction.
Multiply the fraction by 100 to get a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Each added layer multiplies the pass fraction by a number below one, though the gain shrinks as the fraction gets small.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction. The question asks for a percentage, so multiply by 100.
That is the percentage for three layers. The fourth layer halves it.

questions.prompt: The database server misses a patch, so the host layer stops nothing. Only the network layer, which stops 90% of what reaches it, and the application layer, which stops 80%, remain. What percentage of attacks gets past both?
hints: Write the pass fraction of each remaining layer.
The host layer no longer changes the result.
Multiply the two pass fractions and give the answer as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Losing the host layer raises the passage from 0.6% to 2%, more than three times as much, though the other layers still hold.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The network layer lets 0.1 through and the application layer lets 0.2 through, so 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.02, which is 2%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure with the host layer in place. Without it, one fewer factor is multiplied in.
That multiplies the stopped fractions. Use the fractions that pass.

questions.prompt: Three independent layers each stop 90% of the attacks that reach them. What percentage of attacks gets past all three?
hints: Find the fraction that passes one layer.
Multiply that fraction three times.
Convert the result to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Three modest layers can stop all but one attack in a thousand, provided that they fail independently.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each layer lets 0.1 through, so 0.1 × 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.001, which is 0.1%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share that passes one layer.
That is the fraction. As a percentage it is 100 times larger.

questions.prompt: A phishing intrusion steals a password, runs a program on a laptop, takes an administrator's token and encrypts the files. Which list names those four stages in order?
hints: Initial access is the first foothold, and impact is the harm at the end.
questions.onCorrect: Each stage builds on the one before, which is why catching an early one prevents the later ones.

choices.label: Execution, initial access, privilege escalation, impact
Initial access, privilege escalation, execution, impact
Initial access, execution, privilege escalation, impact
Initial access, execution, impact, privilege escalation

acceptedIdeas: Initial access, execution, privilege escalation, impact
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Initial access, execution, privilege escalation, impact

misconceptions.feedback: The password comes first and gives the foothold. A program cannot run on the laptop until the attacker has some access to it.
Running the program precedes taking the administrator's token, which the program makes possible.
Encrypting the files is the harm itself, so impact comes last.

questions.prompt: You want to scan your employer's website for weaknesses. What do you need from its owner before you start?
hints: The test is lawful only if the owner has agreed in advance, and agreed in a form that can be shown.
questions.onCorrect: The permission names the systems, the dates and the methods in scope, so that the test stays inside what the owner allowed.

questions.prompt: A scan of a web server that also holds customer records shows these open ports: 22 (ssh), 443 (https), 5432 (postgresql) and 8080 (http). Which of them is the database, which should not be reachable from the internet?
hints: Find the port that the scan labels with a database's name.
questions.onCorrect: A database reachable from the internet invites password guessing and attacks on the database software itself, so it sits behind the web server.

misconceptions.feedback: Port 22 is ssh, which gives remote command access. It should be limited to administrators' addresses, but it is not the database.
Port 443 carries https, which a web server has to answer from the internet.
Port 8080 here carries http, a second web port, while the database is the postgresql service.

questions.prompt: A firewall's rules, in order, are: 1 deny tcp 5432 from any host to db; 2 allow tcp 5432 from web to db; 3 deny all. What happens to a packet from web to db on tcp 5432?
hints: Read the rules from the top.
Ask whether rule 1 matches a packet that comes from the web server.
questions.onCorrect: A broad rule above a narrow one hides it, so the fix is to put the allow rule for the web server first.

choices.label: Rule 2 allows it, because it names the web server exactly
Rule 1 denies it, because it matches first
Rule 3 denies it, because it ends the list
It is allowed, because an allow rule outranks a deny rule

acceptedIdeas: Rule 1 denies it, because it matches first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rule 1 denies it, because it matches first

misconceptions.feedback: Rule 2 would allow it, but the firewall stops at the first rule that matches, and rule 1, which covers any source, matches first.
The packet never reaches rule 3, because rule 1 already matches it and decides.
A firewall gives no rule priority by kind. It reads from the top, and the first rule that matches decides.

questions.prompt: What is a final rule called that denies all traffic not allowed by an earlier rule?
hints: It reverses the burden of proof for traffic nobody has listed.
questions.onCorrect: With default deny a forgotten rule causes an outage that someone notices, instead of an exposure that nobody does.

questions.prompt: Give the number of the rule that decides the packet from the internet to the web server on tcp 22.
hints: Go down the list in order and ask whether each rule matches.
Rule 3 allows port 22 only for the office network.
No allow rule matches, so the rule that denies everything decides.
questions.onCorrect: An outside host reaches rule 4 because rule 3 names the office as the only source for ssh.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rules 1, 2 and 3 all fail to match, since the port, the destination or the source is wrong, so rule 4, deny all, decides it.

misconceptions.feedback: Rule 3 does name port 22 and the web server, but only for sources in the office network, and this packet comes from outside.
Rule 1 is about tcp 443, and this packet is for tcp 22.

questions.prompt: A café's Wi-Fi uses WEP, hides its network name and filters by device address. Name a protocol that it should switch to for the largest gain in security.
hints: WEP can be broken, and hiding names and filtering addresses do not stop that.
