questions.onCorrect: WPA2 or WPA3 with a long passphrase protects the traffic itself, which the other two measures never did.

questions.prompt: A web server's scan shows open ports 22, 80, 443, 3306 and 3389. Only ports 80 and 443 need to be reachable from the internet. How many of the open ports are surplus attack surface?
hints: List the open ports that are not 80 or 443.
Count them.
The three are ssh, a database and remote desktop.
questions.onCorrect: Each surplus port can be closed or restricted to a trusted address, which shrinks the attack surface without touching the website.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ports 22, 3306 and 3389 are not needed from the internet, which is 3 surplus ports.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total number of open ports. Two of them are needed.
That counts the ports that are needed. The question asks for the surplus.

questions.prompt: Rules in order: 1 allow tcp 80 from any to web; 2 deny tcp 80 from 203.0.113.7 to web; 3 deny all. Is a packet from 203.0.113.7 to web on tcp 80 allowed? Answer yes or no.
hints: Rule 1 is checked first. Does it match this packet?
questions.onCorrect: Rule 1 matches any source, so rule 2 is never reached. The block on that address has to come above the general allow.

questions.prompt: What should the final rule of a firewall rule set be?
hints: Ask what should happen to traffic nobody has listed.
questions.onCorrect: Default deny makes every permitted flow an explicit decision, and anything unlisted is blocked.

choices.label: Deny all
Allow all
Log only
Allow established

misconceptions.feedback: An allow-all rule at the end would let through everything that no earlier rule named, which is the opposite of a safe default.
Logging records traffic but does not stop it. The final rule has to decide what happens to it.
Replies to connections already allowed are handled by stateful tracking, and the final rule is still needed for everything else.

questions.prompt: A table users has 3 rows, and a program builds this query: SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'; Roughly what does it return?
hints: Look at what comes after OR.
Ask whether '1'='1' depends on which row is being tested.
questions.onCorrect: The comparison '1'='1' is true for every row, so all 3 rows come back.

choices.label: No rows, since no user has an empty name
Every row in the table
An error, because the quotes do not pair up

misconceptions.feedback: No row has an empty name, but the condition goes on with OR '1'='1', which is true whichever row is tested, so every row matches.
Every quote in this query has a partner, in '' and in '1'='1', so the database parses it without complaint.

questions.prompt: SQL evaluates one of the operators AND and OR before the other. Which is evaluated first?
hints: In the same way as in arithmetic, one of them binds more tightly, like multiplication.
questions.onCorrect: AND binds more tightly than OR, in the way multiplication does over addition, so a stray OR can override an earlier AND.

questions.prompt: With the typed text compared as plain data, how many of the 4 rows have the password ' OR '1'='1 ?
hints: The database compares the typed text letter by letter with each stored password.
The quotes and the word OR are now just characters in a text value.
Does any stored password equal that whole text?
questions.onCorrect: The login fails safely: the database was asked for a user with that odd password, and none exists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No user chose that exact text as a password, so no row matches and 0 rows are returned.

misconceptions.feedback: That would happen if the text were read as query syntax. As a parameter it is only a value to compare.

questions.prompt: A visitor's comment is a<b. After HTML encoding turns < into < how many characters long is the text that goes into the page?
hints: Count the characters in the replacement < first.
The letters a and b are unchanged.
Add the lengths of the three parts.
questions.onCorrect: The page now contains harmless characters, and the browser draws them as a less-than sign instead of starting a tag.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: a, then < which is 4 characters, then b: 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length before encoding. The replacement for < is longer than one character.
The replacement < has four characters including the semicolon.

questions.prompt: A visitor's comment is a<b, and the page applies HTML encoding before inserting it. What text goes into the page's HTML?
hints: Encoding changes only the characters that mean something to HTML.
Ask which character in a<b has a meaning in HTML, and how the lesson said it is written.
questions.onCorrect: The browser displays < as a less-than sign, so the reader sees a<b as typed while the page's structure stays as the site wrote it.

choices.label: a<b
ab
a<b
a%3Cb

misconceptions.feedback: Inserting a<b unchanged lets the browser read < as the start of a tag, which is the fault that encoding exists to prevent.
Encoding keeps every character the visitor typed and changes only how < is written, so the reader still sees a<b on the page.
%3C is how < is written in a URL. Text placed in the body of an HTML page needs the HTML form, <, which is why the encoding has to suit the place where the text lands.

questions.prompt: A search page prints 'You searched for' followed by the search text taken from the address, without encoding it. A victim follows a link that carries a script in the search text. Is this stored or reflected cross-site scripting?
hints: The script is not saved on the server. Where does it travel?
questions.onCorrect: Reflected XSS bounces off one request, so its victims are the people sent the crafted link, and the fix is the same encoding.

questions.prompt: A table users has 5 rows. A program builds SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = 'Ada' OR 1=1; How many rows does it return?
hints: Check whether 1=1 depends on the row.
OR needs only one true side.
Count the rows for which the whole condition is true.
questions.onCorrect: The attacker's extra condition is always true, so the name test no longer filters anything.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1=1 is true for every row, so the OR is true for every row and all 5 rows are returned.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the row for Ada makes the first test true, but 1=1 is true for every row, and OR needs just one side.
Ada may or may not exist, but 1=1 is true for every row, so rows are returned.

questions.prompt: What is a query called whose text and values are sent to the database separately, so that a value cannot change the query's structure?
hints: The text carries a marker for each value, and the values arrive afterwards.
questions.onCorrect: Markers keep code and data in separate channels, so the database never has to guess where one ends and the other begins.

questions.prompt: Which defence best stops stored cross-site scripting on a comment page?
hints: The fault is in how the stored text is inserted into the page.
questions.onCorrect: Encoding at the point of output works whatever the comment contains, and a Content Security Policy adds a second layer.

choices.label: Rate limiting
Longer sessions
Hiding the comment form
Context-aware output encoding

misconceptions.feedback: Rate limiting slows repeated requests, but a single stored comment still reaches every reader.
Session length has no bearing on whether a comment is inserted as text or as code.
Hiding the form hides the interface, and anyone can still send the request without it.

questions.prompt: In a parameterised query such as WHERE name = ?, what reaches the database first?
hints: The database has to parse the query before it can accept a value for it.
questions.onCorrect: Because the structure is fixed before any value arrives, nothing in a value can alter it.

choices.label: The query text, which is parsed before any value arrives
The value, so that the database knows what to look for
The two together, joined into one string

acceptedIdeas: The query text, which is parsed before any value arrives
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The query text, which is parsed before any value arrives

misconceptions.feedback: The value is supplied afterwards on its own channel, which is why its characters can never change how the query is parsed.
Joining them into one string is the concatenation that causes injection, and a parameterised query keeps them apart.

questions.prompt: Four requests arrive. User 3 asks for invoice 310, which is theirs. User 3 asks for invoice 311, which belongs to user 4. User 4 asks for invoice 311. User 3 asks for invoice 312, which belongs to user 8. A correct server checks ownership on each request. How many of the four does it deny?
hints: Compare the signed-in user with the invoice owner for each request.
Two of the requests are for an invoice the user owns.
Count the requests where the owner differs from the signed-in user.
questions.onCorrect: Each denial is a decision made by the server on that request, and a correct server makes it every time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Invoice 311 is not user 3's, and neither is invoice 312, so those two requests are denied. The other two are for the user's own invoices.

misconceptions.feedback: Two requests are for invoices that belong to someone else: invoice 311 asked for by user 3, and invoice 312.
User 4 asking for invoice 311 is allowed, since it is theirs. Only the requests for other people's invoices are denied.

questions.prompt: A correct server checks ownership on every request. Four requests arrive: (1) user 3 asks for invoice 310, which is theirs; (2) user 3 asks for invoice 311, which belongs to user 4; (3) user 4 asks for invoice 311; (4) user 3 asks for invoice 312, which belongs to user 8. Which requests does it deny?
hints: Compare the owner of each invoice with the user who asks for it.
questions.onCorrect: Each decision compares the invoice's owner with the user asking, so the server needs no list of forbidden requests, only the owner of each object.

choices.label: Only request 2
Requests 2 and 4
Requests 2, 3 and 4
None, since every user is signed in

misconceptions.feedback: Request 4 also asks for an invoice that belongs to someone else, user 8, so it fails the same check as request 2.
Invoice 311 belongs to user 4, so request 3 is the owner asking for their own invoice and is allowed.
Signing in shows who each user is but not which invoices they may see, and the server has to check that on each request.

questions.prompt: A site changes data only through POST requests, sets its session cookie to allow cross-site sending, and has no token. Can a hidden form on another site still send a request that carries the cookie?
hints: The browser attaches the cookie to a form submission whether it is a GET or a POST.
questions.onCorrect: The method makes no difference to whether the cookie is attached, so a token or a SameSite cookie is needed.

choices.label: Yes, since a hidden form can submit a POST and the browser attaches the cookie
No, since a page on another site can send only GET requests
No, since browsers never attach a site's cookies to requests that start elsewhere

acceptedIdeas: Yes, since a hidden form can submit a POST and the browser attaches the cookie
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, since a hidden form can submit a POST and the browser attaches the cookie

misconceptions.feedback: An HTML form can use the POST method, and a hidden one can be submitted by script, so POST is no barrier.
Browsers attach a site's cookies to requests to that site unless the cookie's SameSite setting withholds them, and this cookie allows cross-site sending.

questions.prompt: Which cookie attribute tells the browser not to attach the cookie to requests that begin on another site?
hints: The name says which sites a cookie is sent from.
questions.onCorrect: Strict withholds the cookie from every cross-site request, and Lax withholds it from most of them, including form posts.

questions.prompt: Name the flaw in the server, which answers a typed address for /admin/users without checking who is asking.
hints: The server never asks whether the user is allowed to see the page.
questions.onCorrect: Hiding the link changes only what the browser shows, and the authorisation check has to be in the server.

questions.prompt: A mobile app's API serves orders at /api/orders/ followed by a random 128-bit identifier that cannot be guessed. A user obtains someone else's identifier from a forwarded email and requests that order. Must the server still check that the order belongs to the user?
hints: An unguessable identifier does not say who may use it.
questions.onCorrect: Obscurity only makes an identifier hard to find, and anyone who learns it, from a link or a log, would be let in without the check.

choices.label: Yes, since anyone who learns the identifier would otherwise be let in
No, since an identifier that cannot be guessed is protection enough
No, since the link must have been shared on purpose

acceptedIdeas: Yes, since anyone who learns the identifier would otherwise be let in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, since anyone who learns the identifier would otherwise be let in

misconceptions.feedback: The identifier cannot be guessed, but this user did not guess it: they read it in a forwarded email, so being hard to guess has not kept it secret.
The email was forwarded, so nobody chose to give this user the order, and a link can reach people its owner never meant it to.

questions.prompt: A feature fetches an image from a link that the user types. Which check on the destination is safer?
hints: A list of bad addresses has to anticipate every way of writing them.
questions.onCorrect: A short list of the destinations the feature needs leaves no room for spellings and redirects that a blocklist would miss.

choices.label: No list, as long as the response turns out to be an image
A blocklist of internal addresses that the server must not fetch
An allowlist of the hosts that the feature needs

acceptedIdeas: An allowlist of the hosts that the feature needs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An allowlist of the hosts that the feature needs

misconceptions.feedback: The request reaches its target whatever the response turns out to be, so checking the response afterwards is too late.
A blocklist misses other spellings of the same address and redirects from an allowed host, so an internal address can slip past it.

questions.prompt: A page at /profile?user=88 shows the profile of user 88 to any signed-in user who changes the number in the address. This flaw is:
hints: Ask whether the server checks that the signed-in user may see that profile.
questions.onCorrect: The fix is a check on the server that the signed-in user is the profile's owner, or has a role that allows access.

choices.label: SQL injection
CSRF
Broken access control
A weak password

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing here puts input into a query as code. The server simply returns another user's data when asked.
CSRF needs a forged request sent from the victim's browser. Here the user sends the request personally.
Passwords are not involved. The user is signed in legitimately, and the server fails to check which profile they may see.

questions.prompt: What is the random value called that a server places in its own forms and checks when they come back, so that a forged cross-site request cannot include it?
hints: It is a value only the genuine form carries.
questions.onCorrect: A page on another site cannot read the token, so it cannot add it to a forged request.

questions.prompt: Invoices are numbered 1000 to 1999, a thousand in all, and user 7 owns 12 of them. If the server has no ownership check, how many invoices belonging to other users can user 7 read by changing the number?
hints: Find the total number of invoices.
Take away the ones user 7 owns.
The others are what remains.
questions.onCorrect: A missing check usually exposes every object at once, since one edited number reaches them all.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 1,000 invoices and user 7 owns 12, so 1,000 − 12 = 988 belong to other users.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many user 7 owns, and those they may read. The question asks about the rest.
User 7 owns 12 of the thousand, so those do not belong to other users.

questions.prompt: How many possible passwords are there of exactly 6 characters when each is one of the 26 lowercase letters?
hints: Each position is filled independently.
Each position has 26 choices.
Multiply 26 by itself 6 times, or work out 26^6.
questions.onCorrect: About 309 million sounds large, yet at 10 billion guesses a second the whole space is searched in about 0.03 seconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 6 positions can be filled in 26 ways, so the count is 26^6 = 308,915,776.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 26 × 6. The positions are filled independently, so the choices multiply, 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 × 26.
That uses only five positions. There are six.

questions.prompt: One more random character, from the same 62 symbols, is added to a password. Roughly what happens to the number of possible passwords?
hints: Each password that existed before can be followed by any of the 62 symbols.
questions.onCorrect: This is why length counts for so much: each character multiplies the work, and widening the alphabet raises the base only once.

choices.label: It grows a little, by 62 more passwords
It doubles
It becomes 62 times as large

misconceptions.feedback: Each existing password can be followed by any of the 62 symbols, so every one of them becomes 62 passwords, not one more.
Doubling would be right for a position with two choices. Here the new position has 62 choices, so the count is multiplied by 62.

questions.prompt: What does a ninth character, from the same alphabet of 36 symbols, do to the number of candidates?
hints: Each existing candidate can be extended in more than one way.
questions.onCorrect: The factor is the alphabet size each time, so ten characters have 36 times as many candidates as nine.

choices.label: It adds 36 more candidates.
It multiplies the number by 36.
It doubles the number.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding 36 would be tiny beside 2.8 trillion. Each existing candidate can be followed by any of 36 symbols, so the count is multiplied.
Doubling would add one bit. A symbol drawn from 36 possibilities multiplies the count by 36.

questions.prompt: How many hours does a full search of 36^10 = 3,656,158,440,062,976 candidates take at 10 billion guesses a second? Give the answer to two decimal places.
hints: Divide the number of candidates by the guesses per second to get seconds.
Divide the seconds by 3,600 to get hours.
The seconds come to about 365,616.
questions.onCorrect: One more character lengthened the search from under 3 hours to over 4 days.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds. Divide by 3,600 to give hours.
That divides by 60 only, which gives minutes. Divide by 3,600 for hours.

questions.prompt: Two users choose the same password, and the site gives each a fresh random salt before hashing. What is stored for the two of them?
hints: The salt is mixed into the password before hashing.
Each user has their own salt.
Different inputs to the hash give different outputs.
questions.onCorrect: Because the hashes differ, an attacker who cracks one password learns nothing about the other.

choices.label: Two different hash values
One hash value, shared by both, since the passwords match
No hash values, since a salted password is stored encrypted instead

misconceptions.feedback: Each password is mixed with its own random salt before hashing, so the two inputs differ and so do the hashes.
Salting is added to hashing and does not replace it. The site stores each salt beside a hash of the salted password.

questions.prompt: A fingerprint scan is offered to a site as evidence of identity. Which kind of factor is it?
hints: It is a feature of the person and not something they remember or carry.
questions.onCorrect: Fingerprints cannot be changed if they leak, so they work best combined with a factor of another kind.

choices.label: Something you have
Something you are
Something you know

misconceptions.feedback: The phone that reads the finger is something you have, but the fingerprint itself is part of your body.
A fingerprint is not a secret that you remember, and you leave copies of it on everything you touch.

questions.prompt: How many possible passwords are there of exactly 5 characters from an alphabet of 62 symbols?
hints: Each of the 5 positions has 62 choices.
The choices multiply across positions.
Work out 62^5.
questions.onCorrect: About 916 million candidates, which at 10 billion guesses a second last less than a tenth of a second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 62 × 5. The positions are independent, so the choices multiply.
That uses four positions. There are five.

questions.prompt: At 10 billion guesses a second, how many seconds does it take to try every password of exactly 7 characters from 62 symbols, given that 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208? Give the answer to two decimal places.
hints: Divide the number of candidates by the guesses per second.
The count is about 3.5 trillion and the rate is 10 billion a second.
The answer is a few hundred seconds.
questions.onCorrect: Seven characters fall in under six minutes, and each further character multiplies the time by 62.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in hours. The question asks for seconds.

questions.prompt: How should a service store user passwords?
hints: The method should be one-way, personal to each user, and costly to guess against.
questions.onCorrect: A slow salted hash forces the attacker to work on one user at a time, at a high cost for each guess.

choices.label: Encrypted with one key
As a slow salted hash
In plain text
As a fast unsalted hash

misconceptions.feedback: The key has to be available to the application, so a thief who takes the database often takes the key, and encryption can be reversed.
Plain text exposes every password as soon as the database leaks.
A fast hash lets an attacker test billions of guesses a second, and without a salt one guess tests every user who chose that password.

questions.prompt: A rule says that only the author of a document may delete it. Which kind of model fits the rule better?
hints: The rule depends on the link between this user and this document.
questions.onCorrect: No role can say "author of this document" without one role per document, while an attribute comparison states it directly.

choices.label: Role-based, by giving every writer an author role
Attribute-based, by comparing the user with the document's author
Role-based, with a separate role for the author of each document

acceptedIdeas: Attribute-based, by comparing the user with the document's author
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Attribute-based, by comparing the user with the document's author

misconceptions.feedback: An author role would let every writer delete every document, including other people's, since a role cannot say whose document it is.
A role for each document would multiply roles with every new document, which is the problem that attributes were brought in to solve.

questions.prompt: A cross-site scripting flaw lets a script run in the page and try to read the session cookie. Which cookie attribute stops page scripts from reading it?
hints: The name says that the cookie is for HTTP and not for scripts.
questions.onCorrect: With HttpOnly the script can still act inside the page, but it cannot copy the identifier and use it elsewhere.

questions.prompt: In the authorisation code flow, which party issues the access token?
hints: It is the party that signs the user in.
questions.onCorrect: The resource server only checks a token. The authorisation server, which signed the user in, issues it.

questions.prompt: How many dots separate the three parts of a signed JWT, in the form header.payload.signature?
hints: Count the separators in header.payload.signature.
Three parts have fewer separators than parts.
There are two.
questions.onCorrect: Splitting at the dots gives the three parts, and the first two can be decoded by anyone.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three parts need two separators, so a signed JWT contains two dots.

misconceptions.feedback: Three is the number of parts. Parts are separated by dots, so there is one fewer dot than parts.

questions.prompt: A token expires at 1893456000 seconds, and the receiver checks it at 1893457800 seconds. By how many seconds is the token past its expiry?
hints: Subtract the expiry from the time of the check.
Both times are in seconds.
The difference is a little under two thousand.
questions.onCorrect: The check fails by half an hour, and one failed check rejects the token however good its signature is.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in minutes. The question asks for seconds.
That is the time of the check. Subtract the expiry from it.

questions.prompt: A developer puts a user's password in the payload of a signed JWT, reasoning that the signature protects it. Does the signature keep the password secret from someone who obtains the token?
hints: The payload is only encoded, and the signature detects changes.
questions.onCorrect: Anyone can decode the payload, so secrets must stay out of it, and a signature protects only against changes.

choices.label: No, since the payload is only base64url, which anyone can decode
Yes, since a signed token cannot be read without the key
Yes, as long as the token has not yet expired

acceptedIdeas: No, since the payload is only base64url, which anyone can decode
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since the payload is only base64url, which anyone can decode

misconceptions.feedback: The key is needed to make or check the signature, not to read the payload, which is written in base64url and decodes without any key.
Expiry decides whether a receiver accepts the token. A copy can still be decoded long after it has expired, so the password would stay readable.

questions.prompt: A hospital rule says that nurses may read the records of patients on their own ward, but only during their shift. Which model fits best?
hints: The rule depends on the ward, the shift and the patient, as well as on the job.
questions.onCorrect: Attributes of the user, the record and the time are all compared, which is what attribute-based control does.

choices.label: Role-based alone
Attribute-based
Discretionary only
Anonymous access

misconceptions.feedback: A role can say "nurse", but not "on this patient's ward" or "during the shift", which are facts about the situation.
Discretionary control leaves the owner of each record to grant access, and a ward and shift rule needs a system-wide policy.
Anonymous access applies no rule about who the user is, which cannot satisfy this one.

questions.prompt: A token has iat 1893452400 and exp 1893456000, both in seconds. How many minutes is its lifetime?
hints: Subtract the issue time from the expiry time.
Convert the difference from seconds to minutes.
Divide the number of seconds by the seconds in a minute.
questions.onCorrect: A one-hour lifetime limits how long a stolen token is useful, at the price of renewing it often.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the lifetime in seconds. The question asks for minutes.
That is the lifetime in hours.

questions.prompt: What does the signature of a JWT provide?
hints: Ask what happens if someone changes the payload, and what happens if someone reads it.
questions.onCorrect: Integrity means that a change is detected, and secrecy would need encryption in addition.

choices.label: Confidentiality
Encryption of the payload
Revocation
Integrity, not confidentiality

misconceptions.feedback: The payload is only encoded, so anyone who holds the token can read it.
The signature is added to the payload and does not encrypt it.
A signed token stays valid until it expires, unless the receiver keeps a list of cancelled tokens.

questions.prompt: A Caesar message reads FDHVDU, and the key is a shift of 3. Shift each letter back by 3. What is the plain word?
hints: Move each letter three places earlier in the alphabet.
F moves back to C.
questions.onCorrect: Decrypting reverses the shift with the same key, which is why the key must stay secret even when the method is known.

questions.prompt: At a billion guesses a second, how many seconds does it take to try every 40-bit key? There are 2^40 = 1,099,511,627,776 keys. Give the answer to two decimal places.
hints: Divide the number of keys by the guesses per second.
A billion is 1,000,000,000.
The answer is a little over a thousand.
questions.onCorrect: A 40-bit key falls in under twenty minutes, and each added bit doubles that time.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by a thousand instead of by a billion.
That is the time in minutes. The question asks for seconds.

questions.prompt: In Python, 11 ^ 6 applies XOR to the bits of 11 (1011) and 6 (0110). What number does it give?
hints: Compare the bits column by column.
A result bit is 1 where the two bits differ, and 0 where they match.
Convert the result 1101 back to a number.
questions.onCorrect: XOR with the same key undoes itself, so (11 ^ 6) ^ 6 is 11 again.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: XOR gives 1 where the bits differ: 1011 and 0110 give 1101, which is 8 + 4 + 1 = 13.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 11 + 6. XOR works on bits and not on whole numbers.
That joins the digits. Work on the bits 1011 and 0110.
That is the bit pattern. Its value as a number is different.

questions.prompt: SHA-256 gives 256 bits, and each hexadecimal character stands for 4 bits. How many hexadecimal characters long is a SHA-256 digest?
hints: Divide the number of bits by the bits in one character.
Each character holds 4 bits.
256 divided by 4.
questions.onCorrect: The digest of any input, whether one letter or a whole film, is the same 64 characters long.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 256 ÷ 4 = 64 hexadecimal characters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of bits. Each hexadecimal character covers 4 of them.
That would be 8 bits per character. A hexadecimal character stands for 4.

questions.prompt: Which key signs a message: the private key or the public key?
hints: Only the owner should be able to sign.
questions.onCorrect: Anyone can check the signature with the public key, but only the holder of the private key can produce one.

questions.prompt: Name the use of asymmetric cryptography that lets two parties who have never met agree on a shared key over an open channel.
hints: The two parties combine public values to arrive at the same secret.
questions.onCorrect: The shared key then protects the rest of the conversation with fast symmetric encryption.

questions.prompt: A site stores customers' passwords as base64 text and calls them encrypted. Does base64 protect the passwords from someone who steals the database?
hints: Ask whether a secret is needed to reverse it.
questions.onCorrect: Base64 rewrites bytes as text, and anyone can reverse it, so it is an encoding and not encryption.

choices.label: Yes, since base64 text cannot be read by eye
Yes, provided the thief does not know which encoding was used
No, since base64 uses no key and anyone can reverse it

acceptedIdeas: No, since base64 uses no key and anyone can reverse it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since base64 uses no key and anyone can reverse it

misconceptions.feedback: Base64 looks scrambled to a person, but any program reverses it in an instant, since it only rewrites bytes as letters and digits.
By Kerckhoffs's principle the method must be assumed known, and base64 is recognisable at a glance, so hiding the choice protects nothing.

questions.prompt: The caesar function computes (pos + key) % 26 for each letter, where pos is the letter's place with A = 0. For the letter Y, pos is 24. What does (24 + 5) % 26 give?
hints: Add the key to the position first.
The sum is more than 25, so it wraps past Z.
Take the remainder after dividing by 26.
questions.onCorrect: The remainder is what bends the alphabet into a circle, so that Z is followed by A.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 24 + 5 = 29, and 29 − 26 = 3, so the position wraps to 3, which is the letter D.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum before wrapping. The remainder after dividing by 26 brings it back into the alphabet.
That is the key. The remainder depends on the sum of the key and the position.

questions.prompt: SHA-512 gives 512 bits, and each hexadecimal character stands for 4 bits. How many hexadecimal characters long is its digest?
hints: Divide the bits by 4.
The earlier digest of 256 bits was 64 characters.
Double that result.
questions.onCorrect: The digest length is fixed by the function, whatever the input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 512 ÷ 4 = 128 hexadecimal characters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length for SHA-256. SHA-512 has twice as many bits.
That is the number of bits. Each hexadecimal character covers 4.

questions.prompt: A Caesar message reads WHVW, and the key is a shift of 3. What is the plain word?
hints: Move each letter three places earlier in the alphabet.
questions.onCorrect: With only 25 useful keys, an attacker needs no knowledge of the message to try every one of them.

questions.prompt: After the handshake, TLS protects the data with a fast key that both sides now share. Is that kind of cryptography symmetric or asymmetric?
hints: A single shared key is used by both sides.
questions.onCorrect: Public-key operations are slow, so TLS uses them only to agree on keys and to prove identity.

questions.prompt: A browser trusts Root CA. A server presents a leaf certificate signed by Intermediate CA, and Intermediate CA's certificate is signed by Root CA. How many signatures must the browser verify to trust the leaf?
hints: List the certificates that are not already in the trust store.
The root needs no check, since the browser already holds it.
Each remaining certificate has one signature to verify.
questions.onCorrect: Each link vouches for the next, so trust flows down from the root that the client chose to hold.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The leaf's signature is checked against the intermediate, and the intermediate's signature against the root. The root is trusted because it is already in the store.

misconceptions.feedback: The root's own entry is signed by itself, and the browser trusts it because it is in the store, so it needs no check.
The leaf's signature needs checking, and so does the intermediate's, since the root has not signed the leaf directly.

questions.prompt: A browser trusts Root CA. A server presents a leaf certificate signed by Intermediate CA, and Intermediate CA's certificate is signed by Root CA. Which signatures must the browser verify to trust the leaf?
hints: Follow the chain from the leaf up to the certificate that the browser already trusts.
questions.onCorrect: Each link is a signature by the certificate above it, and the chain stops at the root because trusting the root is a decision already made.

choices.label: Only the leaf's, made by Intermediate CA
The leaf's and the intermediate's, made by Intermediate CA and Root CA
All three, including the root's signature on its own certificate

acceptedIdeas: The leaf's and the intermediate's, made by Intermediate CA and Root CA
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The leaf's and the intermediate's, made by Intermediate CA and Root CA

misconceptions.feedback: The leaf's signature shows only that Intermediate CA vouched for it, and the browser has no reason to trust Intermediate CA until it has checked Root CA's signature on its certificate.
Root CA is already in the trust store and its certificate is signed by itself, so checking that signature would prove nothing new.

questions.prompt: A server at api.example.com presents a certificate for www.example.com. Which check fails?
hints: Compare the name the browser asked for with the name the certificate carries.
questions.onCorrect: A certificate for one name is evidence about that name only, so a mismatch ends the connection.

choices.label: Key length
Expiry
Name match
Signature algorithm

misconceptions.feedback: The key may be perfectly strong. The certificate is a valid statement about a different name.
The dates could be fine. The fault lies in which name the certificate was issued for.
The signature can verify correctly. The certificate simply does not name the site that was asked for.

questions.prompt: The certificate's last valid day was 30 May 2026, and the browser checks it on 2 June 2026. How many days past its expiry is it?
hints: Count the days after 30 May up to the day of the check.
31 May is the first of them.
Stop at 2 June.
questions.onCorrect: Three days late is as unusable as three years late, which is why renewal has to happen before the date.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From 30 May to 2 June is 3 days: 31 May, 1 June and 2 June.

misconceptions.feedback: Count 31 May as well: the days after the 30th are 31 May, 1 June and 2 June.
That counts from the start of May. The question asks only for the days after the 30th.

questions.prompt: A certificate is valid until 30 May 2026. How many days remain on 20 April 2026?
hints: Count the days remaining in April after the 20th.
Add the days of May up to the 30th.
The two parts are 10 and 30.
questions.onCorrect: A monitor that warns at 30 days would have fired ten days ago, which is why many teams alert earlier still.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 10 days left in April after the 20th and 30 days in May up to the 30th: 10 + 30 = 40.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the days left in April. Add the days of May up to the 30th.
That counts only May. Add the days left in April after the 20th.

questions.prompt: A phishing page for a lookalike bank name has a valid certificate for its own name and shows the padlock. Does the padlock show that it is safe to type your bank password into it?
hints: Ask what the padlock actually reports about the connection.
questions.onCorrect: The padlock says that the connection is encrypted to the named site. Whether that site deserves trust is a different question.

choices.label: Yes, since a certificate authority has vouched for the site
Yes, since browsers refuse certificates for lookalike names
No, since it shows only that the connection is encrypted to the name in the address

acceptedIdeas: No, since it shows only that the connection is encrypted to the name in the address
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since it shows only that the connection is encrypted to the name in the address

misconceptions.feedback: The authority checked only that the applicant controls the lookalike name, which a criminal can register as easily as anyone.
A lookalike name is a different, valid name, and the browser checks only that the certificate matches the name in the address.

questions.prompt: When does a client trust a certificate?
hints: Think about where trust starts in the trust store.
questions.onCorrect: The root is trusted because the client already holds it, and each signature extends that trust one link.

choices.label: When a chain of signatures leads to a root it already trusts
When the connection is encrypted
When the site is popular
When the certificate is long

acceptedIdeas: When a chain of signatures leads to a root it already trusts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: When a chain of signatures leads to a root it already trusts

misconceptions.feedback: Encryption can protect a connection to an impostor. Trust comes from the chain of signatures.
Popularity plays no part in the checks. The chain of signatures decides.
The length of a certificate has no bearing on whether it is trusted.

questions.prompt: A certificate is valid from 1 March 2026 to 30 May 2026. How many days after 1 March is 30 May?
hints: Count the days from 1 March to 1 April.
Then add the days from 1 April to 1 May, and on to 30 May.
questions.onCorrect: A 90-day lifetime is common for certificates that are renewed automatically.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: March has 31 days, so 1 April is 31 days after 1 March, 1 May is 61 days after, and 30 May is 90 days after.

misconceptions.feedback: Count 1 March as day 0, and 30 May is the last day counted, which is one more than that.
Count only up to 30 May. 31 + 30 + 29 gives the total.

questions.prompt: What type of organisation signs certificates?
hints: Its initials are CA.
questions.onCorrect: A certificate authority checks that the applicant controls the name, then signs a statement binding the name to the public key.

questions.prompt: A CVSS base score of 9.8 falls in which qualitative band: low, medium, high or critical?
hints: Scores from 9.0 upwards sit in the top band.
questions.onCorrect: The bands are Low 0.1 to 3.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, High 7.0 to 8.9 and Critical 9.0 to 10.0.

questions.prompt: Using the example rule, an internal file server has a flaw scored 5.5 and no attacks have been seen. The weights are 3 for internet-facing, 2 for internal and 1 for isolated, with 10 added if attacks have been seen. What is its priority?
hints: Pick the weight for an internal server.
Multiply the score by that weight.
No attacks have been seen, so nothing is added.
questions.onCorrect: A medium flaw on a shared internal system can outrank a higher score on a system nobody can reach.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The weight for an internal server is 2, so 5.5 × 2 = 11, and nothing is added.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 10 as though attacks had been seen. None have, so nothing is added.
That is the score alone. The exposure weight multiplies it.

questions.prompt: Why does the rule give an internet-facing server a higher weight than an isolated one?
hints: Ask who can attempt an attack against each of the two servers.
questions.onCorrect: Exposure raises the likelihood of an attempt, which is the part of risk that a technical score does not contain.

choices.label: Internet-facing servers always hold more data.
More attackers can reach it, so an attempt is likelier.
Its CVSS score is always higher.

acceptedIdeas: More attackers can reach it, so an attempt is likelier.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More attackers can reach it, so an attempt is likelier.

misconceptions.feedback: The weight is about reach, and holds whatever the data. An internet-facing server may hold very little, yet still be attacked.
The score is the same for the same flaw wherever it sits. The weight accounts for what the score leaves out.

questions.prompt: A sixth finding, F, is a 6.4 on an internet-facing server, and attacks have been seen. The weight is 3, so 6.4 × 3 = 19.2. After adding 10 for the attacks, what is the priority?
hints: Start from the product of score and weight, 19.2.
Attacks have been seen, so add the extra 10.
Add 10 to 19.2.
questions.onCorrect: Evidence of use can lift a middling score to the top of the list, and the list needs to be refreshed as that evidence arrives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 19.2 + 10 = 29.2. Finding B scores 32.5, so F would come second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the product before the extra 10 for exploitation is added.
That adds the score to the weight. The weight multiplies the score.

questions.prompt: A team wants to find a known-vulnerable library in its project before release. Which check does this?
hints: The check compares the project's libraries with a database of known flaws.
questions.onCorrect: A dependency scan works from a list of the libraries and their versions, which is why a software bill of materials helps.

choices.label: Dependency scanning
Static analysis
Secret scanning

misconceptions.feedback: Static analysis reads the team's own source for dangerous patterns, and it does not compare the libraries with a database of known flaws.
Secret scanning looks for passwords and keys committed by mistake, not for flawed libraries.

questions.prompt: A scanner reports no findings on an application. Does that show that the application has no vulnerabilities?
hints: Ask what kinds of flaw a scanner is able to test for.
questions.onCorrect: A scanner looks for known classes of flaw, so a clean report means only that none of those were found.

choices.label: Yes, if the scanner's database is up to date
Yes, since a scanner checks every part of the code
No, since a scanner finds only flaws of the kinds it knows about

acceptedIdeas: No, since a scanner finds only flaws of the kinds it knows about
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since a scanner finds only flaws of the kinds it knows about

misconceptions.feedback: An up-to-date database still holds only flaws already known, and a new flaw in this application's own logic would not be in it.
A scanner looks for the patterns it was built to recognise, and a flaw that matches none of them passes unseen wherever it sits.

questions.prompt: A CVSS base score of 5.3 falls in which band?
hints: Find the range in the list that includes 5.3.
questions.onCorrect: Medium covers 4.0 to 6.9, and the band describes technical severity before any account of exposure.

choices.label: High
Low
Critical
Medium

misconceptions.feedback: High begins at 7.0, and 5.3 is below it.
Low ends at 3.9, and 5.3 is above it.
Critical begins at 9.0, well above 5.3.

questions.prompt: Using the example rule, a flaw scored 7.0 sits on an internet-facing server, and no attacks have been seen. What is its priority? The weights are 3 for internet-facing, 2 for internal and 1 for isolated, with 10 added if attacks have been seen.
hints: Pick the weight for an internet-facing server.
Multiply the score by that weight.
No attacks have been seen, so nothing is added.
questions.onCorrect: Reach alone triples this finding, but evidence of attacks would add a further 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The weight is 3, so 7.0 × 3 = 21, and nothing is added.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 10 as though attacks had been seen. None have, so nothing is added.
That is the score alone. The exposure weight multiplies it.

questions.prompt: Which file, served from the /.well-known/ path of a site, tells researchers where to send a vulnerability report?
hints: It is a plain text file, named for its purpose.
questions.onCorrect: The file gives a contact address and a disclosure policy, and it is described in RFC 9116.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to log the password that was typed in each failed login, to help debugging. Is that safe?
hints: Ask who can read the logs, and where copies end up.
questions.onCorrect: Logs are copied to many systems and read by many people, so a secret written into one is exposed to all of them.

choices.label: Yes, since the passwords in failed logins are wrong ones
No, since logs are copied to many systems and read by many people
Yes, if the log is sent to a separate server

acceptedIdeas: No, since logs are copied to many systems and read by many people
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since logs are copied to many systems and read by many people

misconceptions.feedback: A failed attempt is often the right password with one slip, or the user's password for another site, so it can be nearly as valuable as the real one.
A separate server protects the log from being changed, but the passwords would still be read by everyone with access to it.

questions.prompt: Log: 10:01:02 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:05 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:08 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:11 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:14 OK alice 203.0.113.9. How many failures come before the success?
hints: Read the result column of each line in time order.
The success is the last line.
Count the lines before it that read FAIL.
questions.onCorrect: Four failures three seconds apart is a machine rhythm, followed by a success, which is the pattern of guessing that worked.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four lines read FAIL, at 10:01:02, :05, :08 and :11, and the fifth line, at 10:01:14, reads OK.

misconceptions.feedback: The fifth line is the success. Only the lines before it count.
That counts the gaps between failures. The question asks for the number of FAIL lines.

questions.prompt: Log: 10:01:02 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:05 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:08 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:11 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:14 OK alice 203.0.113.9. What does it most likely show?
hints: Look at the times between the attempts.
Ask what the last line means after the four before it.
questions.onCorrect: The defender now treats alice's account as compromised and looks at everything it did from 10:01:14 onwards.

choices.label: Nothing worth following up, since the last attempt succeeded
Alice mistyping her password a few times
Automated guessing from one address that succeeded

acceptedIdeas: Automated guessing from one address that succeeded
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Automated guessing from one address that succeeded

misconceptions.feedback: A success after a burst of failures is the point at which an intrusion may begin, so it is the line most worth following up.
The attempts come exactly three seconds apart, a steady machine rhythm that a person correcting a typo would not keep.

questions.prompt: A user logs in from London and, 30 minutes later, from New York, which is 5,570 km away. Roughly how fast would the user have had to travel between the two logins?
hints: Think about how long a flight across the Atlantic takes.
questions.onCorrect: 5,570 km in half an hour is 5,570 ÷ 0.5 = 11,140 km/h, more than ten times an airliner's speed, so the two logins cannot be one person travelling.

choices.label: About as fast as a car on a motorway
About as fast as an airliner
Far faster than any airliner

misconceptions.feedback: At motorway speed, 5,570 km would take more than two days, and the two logins are half an hour apart.
A flight from London to New York takes several hours, and the two logins are only 30 minutes apart.

questions.prompt: A rule fires on 5 or more failures for one account within a 120-second window. Failures for an account occur at 0, 20, 45, 80, 110 and 150 seconds. How many of them fall in the window that starts at 0 seconds and ends at 120 seconds?
hints: List the failures whose time is no more than 120 seconds.
The failure at 150 seconds is outside the window.
Count the rest.
questions.onCorrect: The count reaches the threshold of 5, so the rule fires on the fifth failure.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The failures at 0, 20, 45, 80 and 110 seconds are all within 120 seconds, and the one at 150 is not, so there are 5, and the rule fires.

misconceptions.feedback: The failure at 150 seconds falls after the window closes at 120 seconds.
The failure at 110 seconds is inside the window, since 110 is less than 120.

questions.prompt: A rule fires on 5 or more failures for one account within any 120-second window. Failures for an account occur at 0, 20, 45, 80, 110 and 150 seconds. Does the rule fire?
hints: The window can start at any moment, including the first failure.
questions.onCorrect: The rule fires at 110 seconds, when the fifth failure arrives, without waiting for the sixth.

choices.label: No, since the failures are spread over 150 seconds, longer than the window
Yes, since five of them fall between 0 and 120 seconds
No, since the 120 seconds up to the last failure hold only four

acceptedIdeas: Yes, since five of them fall between 0 and 120 seconds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, since five of them fall between 0 and 120 seconds

misconceptions.feedback: The rule asks whether any 120 seconds hold five failures, and the stretch from 0 to 120 seconds holds the failures at 0, 20, 45, 80 and 110.
The window is not tied to the last failure. The stretch from 0 to 120 seconds holds five, so the rule fires when the fifth arrives at 110 seconds.

questions.prompt: How many minutes after midnight is 14:20?
hints: There are 60 minutes in an hour.
Multiply the hours by 60.
Add the 20 minutes.
questions.onCorrect: Working in minutes since midnight turns a time difference into a single subtraction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 14 hours is 14 × 60 = 840 minutes, and adding 20 gives 860.

misconceptions.feedback: That joins the digits of 14:20. Convert the hours to minutes first.
That counts the hours only. Add the 20 minutes.

questions.prompt: An intrusion starts at 22:40 and is detected at 03:10 the next morning. The time from 22:40 to midnight is 80 minutes, and from midnight to 03:10 is 190 minutes. What is the dwell time in minutes?
hints: Add the two parts, before and after midnight.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: Splitting at midnight avoids a negative difference when the detection falls on the next day.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 + 190 = 270 minutes, which is 4 hours 30 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the time after midnight. Add the 80 minutes before it.
That is only the time before midnight. Add the 190 minutes after it.

questions.prompt: An attacker gains administrator access to a web server that keeps the only copy of its log on its own disk. Can the team rely on that log to show what the attacker did?
hints: Ask what an administrator is able to do to files on the machine.
questions.onCorrect: Logs should be sent as written to a separate server that the first machine cannot change, so an intruder cannot edit the record of the visit.

choices.label: No, since an administrator can edit or delete that log to hide the visit
Yes, as long as logging was on before the attack
Yes, since any change to a log is itself logged

acceptedIdeas: No, since an administrator can edit or delete that log to hide the visit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since an administrator can edit or delete that log to hide the visit

misconceptions.feedback: Logging being on means the entries were written, but an attacker with administrator rights can change or remove them afterwards.
A log cannot reliably record its own tampering when the person tampering controls the machine that writes it.

questions.prompt: The first malicious activity is at 08:50 and the detection is at 13:35 on the same day. What is the dwell time in minutes?
hints: Convert each time to minutes after midnight.
The earlier time is 530 minutes.
Subtract the start from the detection.
questions.onCorrect: Each hour of dwell time is another hour in which the later stages of an intrusion can proceed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 08:50 is 530 minutes after midnight and 13:35 is 815, so 815 − 530 = 285 minutes, which is 4 hours 45 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in hours. The question asks for minutes.

questions.prompt: Which of these should never be written to a log?
hints: Ask which of the four is a secret.
questions.onCorrect: Logs are copied widely, so a secret in one reaches everyone who can read it.

choices.label: Timestamps
Outcomes
Plain-text passwords
Usernames

misconceptions.feedback: Timestamps are needed to order events and to measure dwell time.
Outcomes show whether an action succeeded, which a pattern of failures depends on.
Usernames show who acted, which every investigation needs, although they should be handled with care.

questions.prompt: What is it called when analysts see so many alerts that come to nothing that they begin to close them without reading?
hints: The word names a tiredness caused by too many alerts.
questions.onCorrect: Tuning rules so that most alerts matter is part of the defence, since an ignored alert protects nothing.

questions.prompt: A team has no contact list for incident roles and has never tested a restore from its backups when ransomware strikes. Which phase of the lifecycle was neglected?
hints: Think about what has to exist before an incident begins.
questions.onCorrect: Roles, contacts, runbooks and tested backups are made before an incident, and they decide how the first hour goes.

questions.prompt: A laptop is suspected to be compromised. What is the best first step?
hints: The first aim is to stop the spread without destroying evidence.
questions.onCorrect: Isolating the laptop while it stays powered on stops the spread and keeps the contents of memory for the investigation.

choices.label: Wipe it
Reboot it
Isolate it from the network
Ignore it

misconceptions.feedback: Wiping destroys the evidence of how the attacker got in and what else they touched, and the cause may remain elsewhere.
A reboot clears the contents of memory, which may hold the malicious program and its keys, and the machine stays on the network.
Ignoring it leaves the attacker free to spread, and the first priority is to stop that.

questions.prompt: Backups run every 6 hours, at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00. Ransomware encrypts the files at 14:20. If the team restores from the latest backup, how many minutes of work are lost?
hints: Find the latest backup before 14:20.
Work out the time from that backup to 14:20.
2 hours is 120 minutes.
questions.onCorrect: The backup schedule sets the most work that a restore can lose, which is why it is settled in preparation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The latest backup was made at 12:00, and the time from 12:00 to 14:20 is 2 hours 20 minutes, which is 140 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in hours. The question asks for minutes.
That measures from midnight. The last backup before the incident was at 12:00.

questions.prompt: Which phase of the lifecycle does isolating the server belong to?
hints: It stops the spread, before the cause is removed.
questions.onCorrect: Containment comes before eradication, so that the incident stops growing while the cause is still being found.

questions.prompt: A laptop shows a ransom note while the other machines look normal. To stop the spread and keep what is in its memory, should the responder isolate it from the network or power it off? Answer isolate or power off.
hints: Powering off loses the contents of memory.
questions.onCorrect: The machine stays on, so its memory can be captured, and it is cut off, so it can spread nothing.

questions.prompt: During an incident a manager asks the team to wipe a suspected machine at once, to be safe. Is that the right first move?
hints: Think about the evidence, and about where the cause might remain.
questions.onCorrect: Wiping first loses the evidence of how the attacker got in and the scope of what they touched, and the cause may reinfect the clean machine.

choices.label: Yes, since wiping removes the attacker from the machine
Yes, once a backup of its files has been taken
No, since wiping destroys the evidence, and the cause may remain elsewhere

acceptedIdeas: No, since wiping destroys the evidence, and the cause may remain elsewhere
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since wiping destroys the evidence, and the cause may remain elsewhere

misconceptions.feedback: Wiping clears this one machine, but the attacker may hold other machines or a stolen password and can return within the hour.
A copy of the files keeps neither the memory nor the traces of how the attacker got in, and the machine should first be isolated to stop the spread.

questions.prompt: How many main phases does the incident lifecycle of NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 describe?
hints: List the phases from preparation to review.
Containment, eradication and recovery count as one phase.
There are as many as there are stops on the loop.
questions.onCorrect: The fourth phase feeds back into the first, so the lifecycle is a loop, and each incident improves the next response.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity. That is 4.

misconceptions.feedback: Containment, eradication and recovery are one phase of the lifecycle, so they do not count three times.
Preparation comes before an incident and the review comes after, so both are phases.

questions.prompt: Which list gives the phases of the lifecycle in the correct order?
hints: Preparation is first and the review is last.
questions.onCorrect: The order follows the life of an incident, and the last phase feeds the first.

choices.label: Detection and analysis; preparation; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity
Preparation; containment, eradication and recovery; detection and analysis; post-incident activity
Preparation; detection and analysis; post-incident activity; containment, eradication and recovery
Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity

acceptedIdeas: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity

misconceptions.feedback: Preparation comes first, since roles, contacts and backups have to exist before anything is detected.
An incident has to be detected and analysed before it can be contained.
The review comes at the end, after the incident has been contained and recovered from.

questions.prompt: The first malicious activity is at 23:40, and the incident is contained at 02:25 the next morning. How many minutes pass from the first activity to containment?
hints: Split the time at midnight.
There are 20 minutes before midnight.
The 145 minutes after midnight are 2 hours 25 minutes.
questions.onCorrect: The time to contain, like the dwell time, is a measure that a team tries to shorten with better preparation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From 23:40 to midnight is 20 minutes, and from midnight to 02:25 is 145 minutes, so the total is 165 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the time after midnight. Add the 20 minutes before it.
That is only the time before midnight. Add the time after it.

flashcards.front: Which property is lost when ransomware makes files unusable?
flashcards.back: The files cannot be used when they are needed, which is a loss of availability.

flashcards.front: What is the ALE of a $5,000 loss expected 4 times a year, in dollars?
flashcards.back: ALE is the cost of one loss times the yearly rate, 5,000 × 4 = 20,000.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ALE is the cost of one loss times the yearly rate, 5,000 × 4 = 20,000.

flashcards.front: Which function did version 2.0 of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework add?
flashcards.back: Govern, which covers the policies and risk decisions the other five functions serve.

flashcards.front: Which STRIDE threat violates availability?
flashcards.back: Denial of service makes a system unavailable to the people who need it.

flashcards.front: Which property does tampering violate?
flashcards.back: Tampering is an unauthorised change to data or code, which is a loss of integrity.

flashcards.front: Name the four responses to a threat.
flashcards.back: A threat can be removed, reduced, transferred or accepted, and the decision is recorded.

flashcards.front: Which stage lets an attacker keep access after a restart?
flashcards.back: Persistence is the stage at which the attacker arranges to return, for example with a scheduled task.

flashcards.front: Two independent controls each stop 50% of attacks. What percentage gets past both?
flashcards.back: Each lets 0.5 through, so 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25, which is 25%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each lets 0.5 through, so 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25, which is 25%.

flashcards.front: Why is defence in depth better than one strong control?
flashcards.back: Any single control can fail, and the attacker then has to defeat the others as well.

flashcards.front: Which port number does https use?
flashcards.back: Https uses port 443, and plain http uses port 80.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Https uses port 443, and plain http uses port 80.

flashcards.front: When two firewall rules both match a packet, does the first or the last one decide?
flashcards.back: The first matching rule decides, and the rules below it are never consulted.

flashcards.front: Why does hiding a Wi-Fi name not secure the network?
flashcards.back: The name is sent in frames whenever devices connect, so it can be read, and only encryption with a strong passphrase protects the traffic.

flashcards.front: What do you call a query whose text and values are sent separately?
flashcards.back: A parameterised query keeps values apart from the query text, so a value cannot alter the query.

flashcards.front: Why does escaping quotes by hand fall short of using parameters?
flashcards.back: Hand-escaping has to anticipate every special character in every context, while parameters remove the confusion between code and data entirely.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the defence that turns < into < before inserting text into a page?
flashcards.back: Output encoding makes the browser display the characters instead of reading them as markup.

flashcards.front: SSRF is short for ___-side request forgery. Which word fills the gap?
flashcards.back: Server: the server is tricked into making a request that the attacker could not make directly.

flashcards.front: Why is an unguessable identifier not a substitute for an ownership check?
flashcards.back: Anyone who learns the identifier, from a link or a log, can use it, and the server still has to decide who may see the object.

flashcards.front: What must the server check on every request to stop a direct object reference flaw?
flashcards.back: It must check that the signed-in user is allowed to access the specific object that the request names.

flashcards.front: How many possible passwords are there of exactly 4 digits?
flashcards.back: Each of the 4 positions has 10 choices, so there are 10^4 = 10,000.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 4 positions has 10 choices, so there are 10^4 = 10,000.

flashcards.front: What random per-user value is stored beside a password hash?
flashcards.back: A salt makes identical passwords produce different hashes and defeats precomputed tables.

flashcards.front: Why is hashing a password not the same as encrypting it?
flashcards.back: A hash cannot be reversed, while encryption is designed to be undone by anyone who holds the key.

flashcards.front: Which cookie attribute makes the browser send the cookie only over HTTPS?
flashcards.back: Secure keeps the cookie off unencrypted connections, where it could be read in transit.

flashcards.front: How many dots does a signed JWT contain?
flashcards.back: The header, payload and signature are separated by two dots.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The header, payload and signature are separated by two dots.

flashcards.front: What does OpenID Connect add to OAuth 2.0?
flashcards.back: It adds an ID token, a signed statement of who signed in, so that applications can use OAuth for login.

flashcards.front: How many hexadecimal characters long is a SHA-256 digest?
flashcards.back: 256 bits at 4 bits per hexadecimal character is 64 characters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 256 bits at 4 bits per hexadecimal character is 64 characters.

flashcards.front: Which key produces a digital signature?
flashcards.back: The private key signs, and the public key verifies.

flashcards.front: Why should a cipher not rely on keeping its algorithm secret?
flashcards.back: Its strength should lie in the key, which can be changed if it leaks, since an algorithm cannot be kept secret for long and gains from open study.

flashcards.front: What is the property called that stops a stolen server key from decrypting recorded traffic?
flashcards.back: Forward secrecy comes from fresh temporary keys for each connection.

flashcards.front: What does the padlock in the address bar tell you?
flashcards.back: It says that the connection is encrypted to the site named in the address, and says nothing about whether the site is honest.

flashcards.front: Which protocol, published as RFC 8446, protects HTTPS in its current version?
flashcards.back: TLS 1.3 was published as RFC 8446 in August 2018.

flashcards.front: Which CVSS band covers scores from 7.0 to 8.9?
flashcards.back: High covers 7.0 to 8.9, and Critical begins at 9.0.

flashcards.front: Why can a medium-score flaw outrank a critical one when patching?
flashcards.back: Exposure and evidence of attacks decide how likely and how soon a flaw is used, and the score does not contain them.

flashcards.front: What does CVE stand for in the identifier CVE-year-number?
flashcards.back: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a shared name for one publicly known flaw.

flashcards.front: An intrusion starts at 08:00 and is detected at 10:30. What is the dwell time in minutes?
flashcards.back: From 08:00 to 10:30 is 2 hours 30 minutes, which is 150 minutes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From 08:00 to 10:30 is 2 hours 30 minutes, which is 150 minutes.

flashcards.front: What kind of rule alerts when a set number of failures occur for one account in a short time?
flashcards.back: A threshold rule counts events within a time window and fires when the count reaches its limit.

flashcards.front: Why should logs be sent to a separate server as they are written?
flashcards.back: An intruder who controls a machine can edit or delete its local log, but not one held on a server that the machine cannot change.

flashcards.front: Name the four phases of the incident lifecycle in order.
flashcards.back: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity.

flashcards.front: Backups run daily at 00:00 and 12:00. Ransomware encrypts files at 15:00. How many hours of work are lost on restore?
flashcards.back: The latest backup was at 12:00, so the work since then, 3 hours, is lost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The latest backup was at 12:00, so the work since then, 3 hours, is lost.

flashcards.front: Why is a post-incident review blameless?
flashcards.back: A mistake happened inside a system that allowed it, and a team that fears blame hides the facts that the next review needs.
